1	kind: attempt
2	Open question attempted: the core claim (C) for hyperfields with -1 = 1 — "1 ∈ x ⊞ y ⇒ 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy" — or at least the weaker normalized goal 1 ∈ T = x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy when -1 = 1. Settle it: prove it, refute it with an explicit hyperfield, or reduce it to a strictly easier precise statement.
3	
4	Background (results obtained earlier in this attempt; each was proved in full in an earlier report, but re-check anything you rely on):
5	
6	(B1) Conventions. A hyperfield is H = G ∪ {0}, G an abelian multiplicative group, with a commutative, associative multivalued addition ⊞ (sums of several terms are unions over all choices, well defined by associativity), 0 neutral, each a has a unique -a with 0 ∈ a ⊞ -a, reversibility (c ∈ a ⊞ b ⇒ a ∈ c ⊞ -b), and distributivity w(a ⊞ b) = wa ⊞ wb for single elements w. -a = (-1)a with (-1)^2 = 1; possibly -1 = 1. Useful: 0 ∈ A ⊞ B iff A ∩ (-B) ≠ ∅; if c ∈ p ⊞ q then (S ⊞ p ⊞ q) ⊇ (S ⊞ c) ("merging two summands into an element of their sum only shrinks the sum"); H ⊞ a = H for every a; if 0 ∈ S then A ⊞ S ⊇ A.
7	
8	(B2) Normalization. z = 0 is trivial (y = -x, and 0 ∈ x^3 ⊞ -x^3). For z ≠ 0, scaling by -1/z makes the question equivalent to: for nonzero x, y with 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, is 1 ∈ T := x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ?
9	
10	(B3) Quotient hyperfields F/U (F a field, U ≤ F^×) satisfy the implication (lift to representatives x'+y'+z' = 0 and use x'^3+y'^3+z'^3-3x'y'z' = (x'+y'+z')(…) = 0). So Krasner, sign, tropical, phase, triangle, weak sign, and all their ordered-group extensions satisfy it; a counterexample must be a NON-quotient hyperfield. Also: if H satisfies it, so does any extension H ⋊ Γ by an ordered abelian group (leading-term argument).
11	
12	(B4) Computer evidence (exhaustive search, unrefereed): no counterexample among all hyperfields H = G ∪ {0} with |G| ≤ 9 (every abelian group of order ≤ 8, and Z9, Z3×Z3). A counterexample has at least 11 elements.
13	
14	(B5) Composition rule (proved). If 0 ∈ A ⊞ t and 0 ∈ B ⊞ (-t) for sums A, B and an element t, then 0 ∈ A ⊞ B. (From 0 ∈ A ⊞ t, -t ∈ A; from the other, t ∈ B; and 0 ∈ (-t) ⊞ t.) But from 0 ∈ C ⊞ a ⊞ (-a) one can NOT conclude 0 ∈ C in general.
15	
16	(B6) Obstruction to "linear" proofs (proved). Treat x, y as formal monomials and let R_w be the relation 0 ∈ wx ⊞ wy ⊞ (-w) (w a monomial ±x^i y^j). No derivation that only composes relations R_w via (B5) yields 0 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ (-1): term counting forces exactly 4 relations, three of which must be R_1, R_{x^2}, R_{y^2}, and the fourth cannot cancel the 6 unwanted terms. The field identity needs the step x^2y + xy^2 = xy, i.e. contracting the SET x^2y ⊞ xy^2 to its element xy, which hyperfield membership does not allow. So an affirmative proof must use auxiliary witness elements (e.g. elements of 1 ⊞ 1, x ⊞ -xy, …) and the associativity/reversibility relations they satisfy.
17	
18	(B7) Diagonal case (proved). If 1 ∈ x ⊞ x then 1 ∈ T: x^2 ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^3 gives T ⊇ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2, and x ∈ x^2 ⊞ x^2 gives this ⊇ x ⊞ x ∋ 1.
19	
20	(B8) Expansion with a witness (proved). From 1 ∈ x ⊞ y: x ∈ x^2 ⊞ xy, x^2 ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^2y, so x ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^2y ⊞ xy; similarly y ∈ y^3 ⊞ xy^2 ⊞ xy; hence 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ w for some w ∈ x^2y ⊞ xy^2 = xy(x ⊞ y). So 1 ∈ T whenever this w can be taken to be xy (e.g. whenever x ⊞ y = {1}). In general the witness u ∈ x ⊞ y with w = xy·u need not be 1.
21	
22	(B9) Class results (proved). (a) If a ⊞ -a = H for all a ≠ 0 and -1 = 1, the implication holds (xy ⊞ xy = H so T = H). With -1 ≠ 1 in this class it is proved only when one of x^3, y^3, z^3 equals xyz; otherwise OPEN. (b) If -1 = 1, then 0 ∈ xy ⊞ xy, so T ⊇ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy, and the implication follows from the core claim (C): 1 ∈ x ⊞ y ⇒ 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy. If a ⊞ a = {a} for all a, then xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy = {xy} and the implication is EQUIVALENT to (C). (C) is OPEN; a field-of-characteristic-2 proof of it uses (x+y)^2 = x^2 + y^2, a cancellation unavailable in hyperfields. (c) Krasner extensions (-1 = 1, a ⊞ a = {0, a}): T = (x^3 ⊞ y^3) ∪ (x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy). These correspond to projective geometries with a regular abelian collineation group; all known ones are quotients (Desarguesian), so they are not promising for a counterexample. (d) Hyperfields in which a ∈ a ⊞ b for all a, b (every multi-sum contains each of its summands), e.g. Massouros' "a ⊞ b = {a, b, a+b} for b ≠ -a, a ⊞ -a = F" built on a field F, satisfy the implication in the cases checked (if x ⊞ y ∋ 1 because 1 ∈ {x, y} then T contains the cube 1; otherwise the field sum 1 = x^3+y^3+3xy is in T).
23	
24	(B10) Exponent-3 reduction (proved; re-checked independently by three reports). Suppose -1 = 1 and g^3 = 1 for all g ∈ G. Put Q := 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1. Since -1 = 1, y ∈ 1 ⊞ x ⇔ 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, so w := xy ranges over x(1 ⊞ x) = x ⊞ x^2. The normalized target is T = 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ w ⊞ w ⊞ w and 1 ∈ T ⇔ 0 ∈ Q ⊞ wQ ⇔ Q ∩ wQ ≠ ∅. Hence such an H is a counterexample iff there are x ∈ G and nonzero w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with Q ∩ wQ = ∅. This needs 1 ∉ 1 ⊞ 1 (else 0 ∈ Q) and w ≠ 1.
25	
26	(B11) Further facts in the case -1 = 1 (proved). (a) 1 ∈ Q := 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1 (since 0 ∈ 1 ⊞ 1, Q ⊇ 1 ⊞ 0). (b) Hence in the exponent-3 class of (B10) a counterexample needs x and w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with w ∉ Q and w^{-1} ∉ Q (if w ∈ Q then w = w·1 ∈ Q ∩ wQ; if w^{-1} ∈ Q then 1 = w·w^{-1} ∈ Q ∩ wQ), besides 1 ∉ 1 ⊞ 1, w ≠ 1 and Q ∩ wQ = ∅. (c) Four-point form of associativity: for a commutative hyperaddition with -1 = 1 satisfying reversibility, e ∈ (a ⊞ b) ⊞ c ⇔ (a ⊞ b) ∩ (c ⊞ e) ≠ ∅, so associativity is EQUIVALENT to: for all a, b, c, e ∈ H, (a ⊞ b) ∩ (c ⊞ e) ≠ ∅ ⇔ (b ⊞ c) ∩ (a ⊞ e) ≠ ∅ (i.e. "0 ∈ a ⊞ b ⊞ c ⊞ e" is a symmetric 4-ary relation). The structure is the same as a G-invariant S_3-symmetric set of "triangles" {a, b, c} (0 ∈ a ⊞ b ⊞ c) with the 4-point condition. (d) If moreover 1 ⊞ 1 = {0}, then H is a field: taking a = b in (c), (a ⊞ c) ∩ (a ⊞ e) ≠ ∅ ⇔ c = e, so for fixed a the |H| nonempty sets a ⊞ c (c ∈ H) are pairwise disjoint and cover H (d ∈ a ⊞ c for any c ∈ a ⊞ d), hence all singletons. So in a non-field with -1 = 1, D := (1 ⊞ 1) \ {0} is nonempty, and Q = {1} ∪ (1 ⊞ D) is never just {1}.
27	
28	(B12) Idempotent class (a ⊞ a = {a} for all a) (proved): with 1 ∈ x ⊞ y one gets 1 ∈ x^2 ⊞ xy ⊞ y^2 (substitute x ∈ x^2 ⊞ xy, y ∈ xy ⊞ y^2 into 1 ∈ x ⊞ y and merge xy ⊞ xy = {xy}) and 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ x^2y ⊞ xy^2 (same again). The target (C) differs only by having the single element xy in place of the set xy(x ⊞ y) ∋ xy; contraction is not allowed.
29	
30	(B13) Further reductions (proved, elementary). (a) If a hyperfield satisfies the implication, so does every quotient H/U by a subgroup U ≤ G (lift and apply it in H). So a counterexample can be sought "upstairs" in a larger hyperfield. (b) If x ⊞ y = {1}, or one of x, y equals 1, or y = x, the normalized claim holds. (c) Coordinator's computer check (unrefereed): G = F_3^k (k ≤ 3, additive notation), -1 = 1, triangles = {a, b, c} distinct with a + b + c in a subgroup K, plus {a, a, 0}, plus {a, a, c} for c - a in D ∈ {∅, K\{0}, G\{0}}: the only associative members are trivial/degenerate ones, all satisfying the claim.
31	
32	(B14) Dead ends recorded so far: purely "linear" derivations (B6); iterating (B8) with a new witness (the witness again ranges over all of x ⊞ y; no progress); re-bracketing (x ⊞ y)^3 (always produces the block xy(x ⊞ y)); the single-valued "affine line" rule a ⊞ b = {-a-b} on F_3^k (not associative for k ≥ 2); Krasner extensions / projective geometries; classes where sums contain summands; small exhaustive search.
33	
34	Your task. Use the new lens (B11)(c): with -1 = 1, "0 ∈ a ⊞ b ⊞ c ⊞ e" ⇔ (a ⊞ b) ∩ (c ⊞ e) ≠ ∅ and this is symmetric in a, b, c, e; more generally 0 ∈ A ⊞ B ⇔ A ∩ B ≠ ∅ for any multi-sums A, B. So 1 ∈ T ⇔ (1 ⊞ x^3) ∩ (y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy) ≠ ∅ ⇔ (1 ⊞ x^3 ⊞ y^3) ∩ xyQ ≠ ∅ (Q = 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1), and (C) ⇔ (1 ⊞ x^3) ∩ (y^3 ⊞ xy) ≠ ∅. The hypothesis is y ∈ 1 ⊞ x.
35	Ideas to try (pick, push, do not survey):
36	 (a) Find intermediate elements: e.g. pick p ∈ 1 ⊞ x (possibly p = y), q ∈ x ⊞ x^2 = x(1 ⊞ x) (e.g. q = xy), r ∈ 1 ⊞ x^2, etc., and chain 4-point exchanges (each exchange turns a known nonempty intersection into another) until you reach (1 ⊞ x^3) ∩ (y^3 ⊞ xy) ≠ ∅ or the T version. The field proof in characteristic 2 is 1 = (x+y)^2 = x^2 + y^2 and x^3 + y^3 + xy = (x+y)(x^2+xy+y^2) + xy; try to mimic each step with exchanges rather than substitution of sets.
37	 (b) Prove a "Frobenius" statement first: 1 ∈ x ⊞ y ⇒ 1 ∈ x^2 ⊞ y^2 (⊞ something containing 0 that you can control), or 1 ∈ x^2 ⊞ y^2 ⊞ Dxy type statements with D = (1⊞1)\{0}, and then cube.
38	 (c) If the chain keeps failing at one exchange, identify the minimal configuration of triangles (a finite list of "0 ∈ a⊞b⊞c" facts, true and false) a counterexample must contain, and decide whether it is consistent with the 4-point condition — this either finishes the proof or gives a precise blueprint for a counterexample (state it precisely; if you can, complete it to an actual hyperfield and verify all axioms).
39	Report precisely what is proved; a full proof of (C) or of 1 ∈ T for -1 = 1 is a significant partial result.
40

# round3_q3: attempt on the normalized claim 1 ∈ x ⊞ y ⇒ 1 ∈ T = x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy

**Status: not settled.** Nothing below proves or refutes the headline question. What follows is the analysis of routes (a)–(c) and why each one stalls, plus one small precise observation.

## Route (a): the symmetric form with a multiplier c
Let c be any single element. Distributivity gives 0 ∈ cx ⊞ cy ⊞ cz exactly. To relate this relation to the target, cx, cy, cz must be replaced by sums. Suppose c ∈ x^2 ⊞ y^2 ⊞ z^2 ⊞ -xy ⊞ -yz ⊞ -zx. Then cx lies in the sum x^3 ⊞ xy^2 ⊞ xz^2 ⊞ -x^2y ⊞ -xyz ⊞ -x^2z, and similarly for cy and cz.

Substituting these memberships into 0 ∈ cx ⊞ cy ⊞ cz gives 0 ∈ S18. Here S18 is the 18-term sum whose terms are the three cubes, three copies of -xyz, and the six cross pairs m ⊞ -m (m ∈ {x^2y, xy^2, x^2z, xz^2, y^2z, yz^2}).

To reach the target we would need the step 0 ∈ C ⊞ m ⊞ -m ⇒ 0 ∈ C, which fails in general (B5). Choosing c inside a different auxiliary sum (x ⊞ -y, x^2 ⊞ -yz, ...) gives the same pattern: every exact substitution adds terms, and nothing allows them to be removed. Removal is possible only through (B5), which needs a *single* element t together with a separate relation for -t. The cross pairs m ⊞ -m arise inside one relation, not in two separate ones, so (B5) does not apply. **Dead end** for any choice of a single multiplier c.

## Route (b): moving the witness
From (B8) we get 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xyu with u ∈ x ⊞ y. Apply (B8) again to 1 ∈ u^{-1}x ⊞ u^{-1}y. This produces a relation with terms u^{-3}x^3, u^{-3}y^3, u^{-2}xy (twice) and u^{-2}xy·u' with u' ∈ u^{-1}(x ⊞ y).

To combine the two relations by (B5), they must share a single element t, appearing as t in one and as -t in the other. The only candidates are the witness terms, and these have different degrees in u, so no common t exists unless u' = u^{-1}·u, i.e. u' = 1. Requiring u' = 1 is exactly the original problem again. **No progress.**

## Route (c): certificates
I did not construct a consistent partial hyperfield with 1 ∈ x ⊞ y and 1 ∉ T. Per (B4) and (B13c), any such configuration needs at least 11 elements and a non-quotient structure. In the exponent-3 class with -1 = 1, (B10)–(B11) reduce the search to the following statement:

> Find G ∪ {0} with -1 = 1, every g ∈ G satisfying g^3 = 1, satisfying the four-point condition, and containing x and w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with w, w^{-1} ∉ Q = 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1 and Q ∩ wQ = ∅.

## Small observation (proved)
Every derivation of 0 ∈ (target) from 0 ∈ x ⊞ y ⊞ z that only uses
- exact distributivity with single multipliers,
- substitution of memberships into sums, and
- (B5) cancellation with single elements

ends in a sum that *contains* the target's terms as a sub-multiset. To conclude, it would therefore need a contraction or cancellation step that is not available. This extends (B6): auxiliary multipliers c alone do not escape the obstruction. A proof would have to use reversibility to create new relations, not only substitutions.

## Open
- The headline question.
- The core claim (C) for -1 = 1.
- The exponent-3 search problem stated in route (c).

=== END OF ANSWER round3_q3 ===

# round3_q2: the core claim (C) in characteristic 2 (-1 = 1)

**Status: (C) is NOT settled.** This file proves one thing: chains of 4-point exchanges cannot prove (C) on their own. Such chains are the same as gluing scaled copies of the hypothesis triangle, and a counting argument rules them out. So any proof has to bring in genuinely new auxiliary elements (witnesses). If no proof exists, a counterexample must break the specific configuration described in section 3.

## 1. Exchanges are compositions

Assume -1 = 1. By (B11)(c), "0 ∈ a⊞b⊞c⊞e" holds iff (a⊞b)∩(c⊞e) ≠ ∅, and this relation is symmetric in a, b, c, e.

A 4-point exchange only re-reads this symmetric relation. The only way to *produce* a new 4-term (or longer) relation from triangles is to glue two relations along a shared element t. This is the composition rule (B5): from 0∈A⊞t and 0∈B⊞t, conclude 0∈A⊞B (here -t = t).

So a chain built only from the hypothesis triangles {g, gx, gy} (all g ∈ G, coming from y ∈ 1⊞x), using exchanges, is a "linear derivation" in the sense of (B6).

## 2. Proposition: no linear derivation proves (C) when -1 = 1

**Claim.** No linear derivation proves (C).

**Proof.**
1. Suppose a derivation glues k relations R_w = {w, wx, wy} (monomial labels w; repeats allowed) into a tree with k-1 gluings.
2. Each gluing removes 2 terms. The relations contribute 3k terms, so the final sum has 3k - 2(k-1) = k + 2 terms.
3. The target 0 ∈ 1⊞x^3⊞y^3⊞xy has 4 terms, so k = 2.
4. Two relations R_w and R_{w'} share a term only if w' ∈ {wx, wy, wx^{-1}, wy^{-1}, wxy^{-1}, wyx^{-1}}. Gluing them leaves 4 terms of the form w·{…}.
5. For the result to equal {1, x^3, y^3, xy} as monomials, the exponents would have to match. Checking all 6 cases, none does: the glued 4-sets have total degree spread at most 2, but {1, x^3} has spread 3.

So the derivation is impossible. ∎

**Why the field proof does not transfer.** Over F_2 one has 1+x^3+y^3+xy = (1+x+y)(1+x+y+x^2+xy+y^2). This combines the six relations R_1, R_x, R_y, R_{x^2}, R_{xy}, R_{y^2}, which have 18 terms. Reaching 4 terms needs 7 cancelled pairs, but a tree on 6 relations allows only 5 gluings. Closing the extra cycles would need the inference "0∈C⊞a⊞a ⇒ 0∈C", which is invalid in hyperfields.

The same argument covers the weaker target 1∈T, with T = x^3⊞y^3⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy. That target has 6 terms, so k = 4. The 12 terms of four relations, glued in a tree, would have to give exactly {1, x^3, y^3, xy, xy, xy}. The coefficient polynomial would have to be a degree-2 multiple of (1+x+y) matching the field identity, which needs 6 relations, not 4. So this is impossible too, as in (B6).

**Consequence.** Any affirmative proof must use auxiliary existential elements, such as d ∈ (1⊞1)\{0} or witnesses u ∈ x⊞y with u ≠ 1, together with the axioms they satisfy. Exchange chains alone, which are idea (a) of the task, cannot work.

## 3. What a counterexample would need (exponent-3, char-2 class)

Combining (B10) and (B11), a counterexample in this class needs all of the following:
- 1 ∉ 1⊞1;
- an element x and some w ∈ x⊞x^2 with w ≠ 1;
- w ∉ Q and w^{-1} ∉ Q, where Q = 1⊞1⊞1 = {1} ∪ (1⊞D) and D = (1⊞1)\{0} ≠ ∅;
- Q ∩ wQ = ∅;
- the triangle set must be G-invariant and satisfy the 4-point condition.

I did not build such a hyperfield, and I did not rule one out. The exhaustive search in (B4) suggests any counterexample has at least 11 elements.

## 4. Open questions

- Is (C) true for hyperfields with -1 = 1? This is open.
- Is the original implication true? This is open in general.
- Does the configuration in section 3 extend to an associative hyperfield? This is open.

=== END OF ANSWER round3_q2 ===

# round3_q4 — partial answer (the main question is still open)

Conventions are those of (B1)/(B2). Normalized form: x, y are nonzero, 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, and T = x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy. The goal is 1 ∈ T, or equivalently 0 ∈ T ⊞ (-1).

## 1. Coincidences in the class a ⊞ -a = H (proved)

Let H be a hyperfield with a ⊞ -a = H for every a ≠ 0.

**Lemma 1.** Let S be a multi-sum whose summands include two nonzero opposite elements a and -a. Then S = H.

*Proof.* Write S = (a ⊞ -a) ⊞ R = H ⊞ R. We have H ⊞ r = H for every element r: given h, pick h' ∈ h ⊞ -r; by reversibility h ∈ h' ⊞ r. Applying this to each summand of R gives S = H. ∎

**Corollary.** If two of the summands of T ⊞ (-1) are opposite, namely the summands x^3, y^3, xy, xy, xy, -1, then T ⊞ (-1) = H ∋ 0 and the claim holds. So the claim holds whenever one of the following holds:
- x^3 = -y^3,
- x^3 = 1 or y^3 = 1 (opposite to -1),
- xy = 1,
- xy = -x^3, i.e. y = -x^2,
- xy = -y^3, i.e. x = -y^2,
- xy = -xy, which is impossible because -1 ≠ 1.

Only the "generic" case remains, where none of these coincidences occurs. In that case xy ⊞ xy does not contain 0, because 0 ∈ a ⊞ a forces a = -a. So nothing more can be extracted from Lemma 1. I could not settle this generic case.

## 2. A natural family in this class satisfies the claim (proved)

**Construction.** Let G be any abelian group containing an element -1 of order 2. Put H = G ∪ {0}, with 0 neutral, and for nonzero a, b define:
- a ⊞ b = {a, b} if b ≠ -a (in particular a ⊞ a = {a});
- a ⊞ -a = H.

**Claim.** H is a hyperfield.

*Proof.* Every multi-sum is computed as follows. If the nonzero summands contain an opposite pair, the sum is H. Otherwise it is the set of the distinct nonzero summands, or {0} if every summand is 0. This rule gives the same set under every bracketing, so ⊞ is associative. It is also commutative.

Reversibility: suppose c ∈ a ⊞ b with a, b ≠ 0.
- If b = -a, then c is arbitrary, and a ∈ c ⊞ a in each subcase c = 0, c = a, c = -a, or c generic, where c ⊞ a = {c, a}.
- If b = a, then c = a, and a ∈ a ⊞ -a = H.
- Otherwise c ∈ {a, b}. If c = a, then a ∈ a ⊞ -b = {a, -b}. If c = b, then a ∈ b ⊞ -b = H.

The cases where a or b is 0 are trivial. Distributivity holds because multiplication by w maps opposite pairs to opposite pairs. ∎

The sign hyperfield is the case G = {±1}.

**Claim.** The implication holds in this H.

*Proof.* Suppose 1 ∈ x ⊞ y with x, y ≠ 0. Then either y = -x or 1 ∈ {x, y}.
- If y = -x, then x^3 and y^3 are opposite, so T = H.
- If x = 1 or y = 1, then 1 is a summand of T. So T is either H or the set of its summands, and either way 1 ∈ T. ∎

So "union-type" hyperfields in this class satisfy the claim. A counterexample must have sums that are genuinely larger than the set of summands but smaller than H.

## 3. Why the generic case resists (recorded obstacle)

Choosing the element 1 in each factor of x(x ⊞ y) and y(x ⊞ y) gives 1 ∈ x^2 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ y^2. Doing it once more gives 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^2y ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy^2 ⊞ y^3. To reach T, the set x^2y ⊞ xy^2 = xy(x ⊞ y) would have to be replaced by its element xy, which is contraction, not containment. This is the same obstacle as (B6) and (B8). The hypothesis a ⊞ -a = H does not help in the generic case, because then no opposite pair occurs among the summands.

## Status

- **Proved:** Lemma 1 and the list of coincidences that make T = H in the class a ⊞ -a = H. Also that the union-type hyperfields of Section 2 (a hyperfield for every G with -1 ≠ 1) satisfy the implication.
- **Open:** the generic case of the class a ⊞ -a = H with -1 ≠ 1. That is: x, y with 1 ∈ x ⊞ y and none of x^3 = -y^3, x^3 = 1, y^3 = 1, xy = 1, y = -x^2, x = -y^2.
- **Open:** part (ii). No counterexample with -1 ≠ 1 was constructed, and no candidate was verified. The headline question remains open.

=== END OF ANSWER round3_q4 ===

# round3_q1: the exponent-3 class with -1 = 1 (partial result)

**Verdict.** I did not settle the question. I found no counterexample and no impossibility proof. Below are (1) the exact translation of the problem into conditions on triangles, and (2) a new proved obstruction: the "linear" derivations of (B6) still fail in the exponent-3 class, even though the extra coincidences x^3 = w^3 = 1 make the parity (mod 2) version solvable. The main question stays open.

## 1. Translation (proved, elementary)

Write G = F_3^k additively. Group element g stands for the multiplicative element, and the hyperfield zero is written ∞. Let Δ be the set of unordered triples {a,b,c} of elements of G, with repetition allowed, such that 0_H ∈ a⊞b⊞c.

**Statement.** By (B11c), the hyperfields of this class are exactly the families Δ that satisfy all of the following:
- Δ is invariant under translation by G;
- membership does not depend on the order of a, b, c;
- the 4-point condition holds.

Here a⊞b = {c ∈ G : {a,b,c} ∈ Δ}, with ∞ added when a = b. Put S_g := 1⊞g ∩ G = {h : {0,g,h} ∈ Δ} and D = S_0.

**Rules for the sets S_g.** Translation invariance and symmetry are equivalent to:

h ∈ S_g ⇔ g ∈ S_h ⇔ −g ∈ S_{h−g} ⇔ −h ∈ S_{g−h}.

These are the six images of {0,g,h} under the affine maps that permute the three points. They determine Δ completely.

**Counterexample condition, by (B10)/(B11).** Define
- Q = {0} ∪ ⋃_{d∈D} S_d,
- w with {x, 2x, w} ∈ Δ for some x,
- and require Q ∩ (w+Q) = ∅.

## 2. Linear derivations fail in the exponent-3 class (proved)

**Admissible moves.** Only the following moves are allowed:
- the relations 0 ∈ mx ⊞ mx² ⊞ mw, for monomials m = x^i w^j;
- the pairs 0 ∈ a⊞a;
- disjoint union of zero-sums (if 0 ∈ A and 0 ∈ B then 0 ∈ A⊞B);
- composition (B5), which cancels one shared term between two different components.

Cancelling a term inside a single component is not allowed (see B5).

**Claim.** In the generic situation, where the 9 monomials x^i w^j are distinct, no such derivation produces 0 ∈ 1⊞1⊞1⊞w⊞w⊞w. (Specific Δ might create extra coincidences among the monomials; that case is not covered.)

**Proof.**

*Step 1 (counting).* A component built from n triangles linked in a tree has n+2 remaining terms. A pair component has 2 terms. Attaching a pair to an existing term changes nothing, because 0∈A⊞a together with 0∈a⊞a gives back 0∈A⊞a. To get 6 terms, the possible shapes are:
- (i) a single tree of 4 triangles;
- (ii) a tree of 2 triangles plus one pair;
- (iii) two separate triangles.

*Step 2 (shapes (ii) and (iii)).* Each triangle has 3 distinct terms. Shape (ii) would need three equal leftover terms from two triangles; shape (iii) would need a triangle {1,1,w} or {1,w,w}. Both are impossible.

*Step 3 (shape (i), reduction to the group ring).* Reduce mod 2 in R = F_2[x,w]/(x³−1, w³−1) ≅ (F_2 × F_4)⊗(F_2 × F_4). Let f be the sum of the four chosen m's. Then f·(x+x²+w) = 1+w + 2(cancelled pairs) ≡ 1+w.

*Step 4 (solving at x = 1).* At x = 1 we have x+x² = 0. The equation becomes f(1,w)·w = 1+w, so f(1,w) = 1+w².

*Step 5 (solving at x = ω).* At x = ω we have x+x² = 1. The equation becomes f(ω,w)(1+w) = 1+w, so f(ω,w) ≡ 1 mod (1+w+w²).

*Step 6 (all solutions).* Write f = a + b w + c w². The conditions give a = 1, b = 0, c = 1+x+x², up to the kernel, which is h(x)(1+w+w²) with h ∈ {0, x+x², 1+x, 1+x²}. So the solutions are

f = 1 + (1+x+x²)w² + h(x)(1+w+w²).

The 4-term solutions include:
- {1, w², xw², x²w²};
- x + (1+x)w + x²w², i.e. {x, w, xw, x²w²}.

*Step 7 (checking multiplicities).* Expand the integer multiset of terms for either 4-term solution. It contains 1 and w exactly once each, and five other monomials exactly twice each. For example, the first solution gives x, x², xw², x²w², w² twice each. The target 1,1,1,w,w,w needs coefficient 3 on both 1 and w. Moreover, 3 tree edges can cancel only 3 of the 5 doubled pairs. So shape (i) fails as well. ∎

**Interpretation.** Unlike the generic case (B6), the mod-2 equation is solvable here. The obstruction comes from the integer multiplicities and the tree structure, not from parity. An affirmative proof would need witnesses from D = (1⊞1)\{0} or other auxiliary elements.

## 3. What is open

- **Construction step not done.** I did not carry out plan steps 2 and 3. I derived no further necessary conditions from the 4-point condition, and I built no explicit Δ on F_3^k with k ≥ 3.
- **Exponent-3 question.** Is there a Δ on G = F_3^k (k ≥ 3) or on F_3^(N) satisfying the rules of §1 and the 4-point condition, with Q ∩ (w+Q) = ∅ for some admissible w? This is OPEN.
- **Headline question.** OPEN.

# round3_q1: the exponent-3 class with -1 = 1 (partial result)

**Verdict.** I did not settle the question. I found no counterexample and no impossibility proof. Below are (1) the exact translation of the problem into conditions on triangles, and (2) a new proved obstruction: the "linear" derivations of (B6) still fail in the exponent-3 class, even though the extra coincidences x^3 = w^3 = 1 make the parity (mod 2) version solvable. The main question stays open.

## 1. Translation (proved, elementary)

Write G = F_3^k additively. Group element g stands for the multiplicative element, and the hyperfield zero is written ∞. Let Δ be the set of unordered triples {a,b,c} of elements of G, with repetition allowed, such that 0_H ∈ a⊞b⊞c.

**Statement.** By (B11c), the hyperfields of this class are exactly the families Δ that satisfy all of the following:
- Δ is invariant under translation by G;
- membership does not depend on the order of a, b, c;
- the 4-point condition holds.

Here a⊞b = {c ∈ G : {a,b,c} ∈ Δ}, with ∞ added when a = b. Put S_g := 1⊞g ∩ G = {h : {0,g,h} ∈ Δ} and D = S_0.

**Rules for the sets S_g.** Translation invariance and symmetry are equivalent to:

h ∈ S_g ⇔ g ∈ S_h ⇔ −g ∈ S_{h−g} ⇔ −h ∈ S_{g−h}.

These are the six images of {0,g,h} under the affine maps that permute the three points. They determine Δ completely.

**Counterexample condition, by (B10)/(B11).** Define
- Q = {0} ∪ ⋃_{d∈D} S_d,
- w with {x, 2x, w} ∈ Δ for some x,
- and require Q ∩ (w+Q) = ∅.

## 2. Linear derivations fail in the exponent-3 class (proved)

**Admissible moves.** Only the following moves are allowed:
- the relations 0 ∈ mx ⊞ mx² ⊞ mw, for monomials m = x^i w^j;
- the pairs 0 ∈ a⊞a;
- disjoint union of zero-sums (if 0 ∈ A and 0 ∈ B then 0 ∈ A⊞B);
- composition (B5), which cancels one shared term between two different components.

Cancelling a term inside a single component is not allowed (see B5).

**Claim.** In the generic situation, where the 9 monomials x^i w^j are distinct, no such derivation produces 0 ∈ 1⊞1⊞1⊞w⊞w⊞w. (Specific Δ might create extra coincidences among the monomials; that case is not covered.)

**Proof.**

*Step 1 (counting).* A component built from n triangles linked in a tree has n+2 remaining terms. A pair component has 2 terms. Attaching a pair to an existing term changes nothing, because 0∈A⊞a together with 0∈a⊞a gives back 0∈A⊞a. To get 6 terms, the possible shapes are:
- (i) a single tree of 4 triangles;
- (ii) a tree of 2 triangles plus one pair;
- (iii) two separate triangles.

*Step 2 (shapes (ii) and (iii)).* Each triangle has 3 distinct terms. Shape (ii) would need three equal leftover terms from two triangles; shape (iii) would need a triangle {1,1,w} or {1,w,w}. Both are impossible.

*Step 3 (shape (i), reduction to the group ring).* Reduce mod 2 in R = F_2[x,w]/(x³−1, w³−1) ≅ (F_2 × F_4)⊗(F_2 × F_4). Let f be the sum of the four chosen m's. Then f·(x+x²+w) = 1+w + 2(cancelled pairs) ≡ 1+w.

*Step 4 (solving at x = 1).* At x = 1 we have x+x² = 0. The equation becomes f(1,w)·w = 1+w, so f(1,w) = 1+w².

*Step 5 (solving at x = ω).* At x = ω we have x+x² = 1. The equation becomes f(ω,w)(1+w) = 1+w, so f(ω,w) ≡ 1 mod (1+w+w²).

*Step 6 (all solutions).* Write f = a + b w + c w². The conditions give a = 1, b = 0, c = 1+x+x², up to the kernel, which is h(x)(1+w+w²) with h ∈ {0, x+x², 1+x, 1+x²}. So the solutions are

f = 1 + (1+x+x²)w² + h(x)(1+w+w²).

The 4-term solutions include:
- {1, w², xw², x²w²};
- x + (1+x)w + x²w², i.e. {x, w, xw, x²w²}.

*Step 7 (checking multiplicities).* Expand the integer multiset of terms for either 4-term solution. It contains 1 and w exactly once each, and five other monomials exactly twice each. For example, the first solution gives x, x², xw², x²w², w² twice each. The target 1,1,1,w,w,w needs coefficient 3 on both 1 and w. Moreover, 3 tree edges can cancel only 3 of the 5 doubled pairs. So shape (i) fails as well. ∎

**Interpretation.** Unlike the generic case (B6), the mod-2 equation is solvable here. The obstruction comes from the integer multiplicities and the tree structure, not from parity. An affirmative proof would need witnesses from D = (1⊞1)\{0} or other auxiliary elements.

## 3. What is open

- **Construction step not done.** I did not carry out plan steps 2 and 3. I derived no further necessary conditions from the 4-point condition, and I built no explicit Δ on F_3^k with k ≥ 3.
- **Exponent-3 question.** Is there a Δ on G = F_3^k (k ≥ 3) or on F_3^(N) satisfying the rules of §1 and the 4-point condition, with Q ∩ (w+Q) = ∅ for some admissible w? This is OPEN.
- **Headline question.** OPEN.

# round3_q2: the core claim (C) in characteristic 2 (-1 = 1)

**Status: (C) is NOT settled.** This file proves one thing: chains of 4-point exchanges cannot prove (C) on their own. Such chains are the same as gluing scaled copies of the hypothesis triangle, and a counting argument rules them out. So any proof has to bring in genuinely new auxiliary elements (witnesses). If no proof exists, a counterexample must break the specific configuration described in section 3.

## 1. Exchanges are compositions

Assume -1 = 1. By (B11)(c), "0 ∈ a⊞b⊞c⊞e" holds iff (a⊞b)∩(c⊞e) ≠ ∅, and this relation is symmetric in a, b, c, e.

A 4-point exchange only re-reads this symmetric relation. The only way to *produce* a new 4-term (or longer) relation from triangles is to glue two relations along a shared element t. This is the composition rule (B5): from 0∈A⊞t and 0∈B⊞t, conclude 0∈A⊞B (here -t = t).

So a chain built only from the hypothesis triangles {g, gx, gy} (all g ∈ G, coming from y ∈ 1⊞x), using exchanges, is a "linear derivation" in the sense of (B6).

## 2. Proposition: no linear derivation proves (C) when -1 = 1

**Claim.** No linear derivation proves (C).

**Proof.**
1. Suppose a derivation glues k relations R_w = {w, wx, wy} (monomial labels w; repeats allowed) into a tree with k-1 gluings.
2. Each gluing removes 2 terms. The relations contribute 3k terms, so the final sum has 3k - 2(k-1) = k + 2 terms.
3. The target 0 ∈ 1⊞x^3⊞y^3⊞xy has 4 terms, so k = 2.
4. Two relations R_w and R_{w'} share a term only if w' ∈ {wx, wy, wx^{-1}, wy^{-1}, wxy^{-1}, wyx^{-1}}. Gluing them leaves 4 terms of the form w·{…}.
5. For the result to equal {1, x^3, y^3, xy} as monomials, the exponents would have to match. Checking all 6 cases, none does: the glued 4-sets have total degree spread at most 2, but {1, x^3} has spread 3.

So the derivation is impossible. ∎

**Why the field proof does not transfer.** Over F_2 one has 1+x^3+y^3+xy = (1+x+y)(1+x+y+x^2+xy+y^2). This combines the six relations R_1, R_x, R_y, R_{x^2}, R_{xy}, R_{y^2}, which have 18 terms. Reaching 4 terms needs 7 cancelled pairs, but a tree on 6 relations allows only 5 gluings. Closing the extra cycles would need the inference "0∈C⊞a⊞a ⇒ 0∈C", which is invalid in hyperfields.

The same argument covers the weaker target 1∈T, with T = x^3⊞y^3⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy. That target has 6 terms, so k = 4. The 12 terms of four relations, glued in a tree, would have to give exactly {1, x^3, y^3, xy, xy, xy}. The coefficient polynomial would have to be a degree-2 multiple of (1+x+y) matching the field identity, which needs 6 relations, not 4. So this is impossible too, as in (B6).

**Consequence.** Any affirmative proof must use auxiliary existential elements, such as d ∈ (1⊞1)\{0} or witnesses u ∈ x⊞y with u ≠ 1, together with the axioms they satisfy. Exchange chains alone, which are idea (a) of the task, cannot work.

## 3. What a counterexample would need (exponent-3, char-2 class)

Combining (B10) and (B11), a counterexample in this class needs all of the following:
- 1 ∉ 1⊞1;
- an element x and some w ∈ x⊞x^2 with w ≠ 1;
- w ∉ Q and w^{-1} ∉ Q, where Q = 1⊞1⊞1 = {1} ∪ (1⊞D) and D = (1⊞1)\{0} ≠ ∅;
- Q ∩ wQ = ∅;
- the triangle set must be G-invariant and satisfy the 4-point condition.

I did not build such a hyperfield, and I did not rule one out. The exhaustive search in (B4) suggests any counterexample has at least 11 elements.

## 4. Open questions

- Is (C) true for hyperfields with -1 = 1? This is open.
- Is the original implication true? This is open in general.
- Does the configuration in section 3 extend to an associative hyperfield? This is open.

# round3_q3: attempt on the normalized claim 1 ∈ x ⊞ y ⇒ 1 ∈ T = x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy

**Status: not settled.** Nothing below proves or refutes the headline question. What follows is the analysis of routes (a)–(c) and why each one stalls, plus one small precise observation.

## Route (a): the symmetric form with a multiplier c
Let c be any single element. Distributivity gives 0 ∈ cx ⊞ cy ⊞ cz exactly. To relate this relation to the target, cx, cy, cz must be replaced by sums. Suppose c ∈ x^2 ⊞ y^2 ⊞ z^2 ⊞ -xy ⊞ -yz ⊞ -zx. Then cx lies in the sum x^3 ⊞ xy^2 ⊞ xz^2 ⊞ -x^2y ⊞ -xyz ⊞ -x^2z, and similarly for cy and cz.

Substituting these memberships into 0 ∈ cx ⊞ cy ⊞ cz gives 0 ∈ S18. Here S18 is the 18-term sum whose terms are the three cubes, three copies of -xyz, and the six cross pairs m ⊞ -m (m ∈ {x^2y, xy^2, x^2z, xz^2, y^2z, yz^2}).

To reach the target we would need the step 0 ∈ C ⊞ m ⊞ -m ⇒ 0 ∈ C, which fails in general (B5). Choosing c inside a different auxiliary sum (x ⊞ -y, x^2 ⊞ -yz, ...) gives the same pattern: every exact substitution adds terms, and nothing allows them to be removed. Removal is possible only through (B5), which needs a *single* element t together with a separate relation for -t. The cross pairs m ⊞ -m arise inside one relation, not in two separate ones, so (B5) does not apply. **Dead end** for any choice of a single multiplier c.

## Route (b): moving the witness
From (B8) we get 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xyu with u ∈ x ⊞ y. Apply (B8) again to 1 ∈ u^{-1}x ⊞ u^{-1}y. This produces a relation with terms u^{-3}x^3, u^{-3}y^3, u^{-2}xy (twice) and u^{-2}xy·u' with u' ∈ u^{-1}(x ⊞ y).

To combine the two relations by (B5), they must share a single element t, appearing as t in one and as -t in the other. The only candidates are the witness terms, and these have different degrees in u, so no common t exists unless u' = u^{-1}·u, i.e. u' = 1. Requiring u' = 1 is exactly the original problem again. **No progress.**

## Route (c): certificates
I did not construct a consistent partial hyperfield with 1 ∈ x ⊞ y and 1 ∉ T. Per (B4) and (B13c), any such configuration needs at least 11 elements and a non-quotient structure. In the exponent-3 class with -1 = 1, (B10)–(B11) reduce the search to the following statement:

> Find G ∪ {0} with -1 = 1, every g ∈ G satisfying g^3 = 1, satisfying the four-point condition, and containing x and w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with w, w^{-1} ∉ Q = 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1 and Q ∩ wQ = ∅.

## Small observation (proved)
Every derivation of 0 ∈ (target) from 0 ∈ x ⊞ y ⊞ z that only uses
- exact distributivity with single multipliers,
- substitution of memberships into sums, and
- (B5) cancellation with single elements

ends in a sum that *contains* the target's terms as a sub-multiset. To conclude, it would therefore need a contraction or cancellation step that is not available. This extends (B6): auxiliary multipliers c alone do not escape the obstruction. A proof would have to use reversibility to create new relations, not only substitutions.

## Open
- The headline question.
- The core claim (C) for -1 = 1.
- The exponent-3 search problem stated in route (c).

# round3_q4 — partial answer (the main question is still open)

Conventions are those of (B1)/(B2). Normalized form: x, y are nonzero, 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, and T = x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy. The goal is 1 ∈ T, or equivalently 0 ∈ T ⊞ (-1).

## 1. Coincidences in the class a ⊞ -a = H (proved)

Let H be a hyperfield with a ⊞ -a = H for every a ≠ 0.

**Lemma 1.** Let S be a multi-sum whose summands include two nonzero opposite elements a and -a. Then S = H.

*Proof.* Write S = (a ⊞ -a) ⊞ R = H ⊞ R. We have H ⊞ r = H for every element r: given h, pick h' ∈ h ⊞ -r; by reversibility h ∈ h' ⊞ r. Applying this to each summand of R gives S = H. ∎

**Corollary.** If two of the summands of T ⊞ (-1) are opposite, namely the summands x^3, y^3, xy, xy, xy, -1, then T ⊞ (-1) = H ∋ 0 and the claim holds. So the claim holds whenever one of the following holds:
- x^3 = -y^3,
- x^3 = 1 or y^3 = 1 (opposite to -1),
- xy = 1,
- xy = -x^3, i.e. y = -x^2,
- xy = -y^3, i.e. x = -y^2,
- xy = -xy, which is impossible because -1 ≠ 1.

Only the "generic" case remains, where none of these coincidences occurs. In that case xy ⊞ xy does not contain 0, because 0 ∈ a ⊞ a forces a = -a. So nothing more can be extracted from Lemma 1. I could not settle this generic case.

## 2. A natural family in this class satisfies the claim (proved)

**Construction.** Let G be any abelian group containing an element -1 of order 2. Put H = G ∪ {0}, with 0 neutral, and for nonzero a, b define:
- a ⊞ b = {a, b} if b ≠ -a (in particular a ⊞ a = {a});
- a ⊞ -a = H.

**Claim.** H is a hyperfield.

*Proof.* Every multi-sum is computed as follows. If the nonzero summands contain an opposite pair, the sum is H. Otherwise it is the set of the distinct nonzero summands, or {0} if every summand is 0. This rule gives the same set under every bracketing, so ⊞ is associative. It is also commutative.

Reversibility: suppose c ∈ a ⊞ b with a, b ≠ 0.
- If b = -a, then c is arbitrary, and a ∈ c ⊞ a in each subcase c = 0, c = a, c = -a, or c generic, where c ⊞ a = {c, a}.
- If b = a, then c = a, and a ∈ a ⊞ -a = H.
- Otherwise c ∈ {a, b}. If c = a, then a ∈ a ⊞ -b = {a, -b}. If c = b, then a ∈ b ⊞ -b = H.

The cases where a or b is 0 are trivial. Distributivity holds because multiplication by w maps opposite pairs to opposite pairs. ∎

The sign hyperfield is the case G = {±1}.

**Claim.** The implication holds in this H.

*Proof.* Suppose 1 ∈ x ⊞ y with x, y ≠ 0. Then either y = -x or 1 ∈ {x, y}.
- If y = -x, then x^3 and y^3 are opposite, so T = H.
- If x = 1 or y = 1, then 1 is a summand of T. So T is either H or the set of its summands, and either way 1 ∈ T. ∎

So "union-type" hyperfields in this class satisfy the claim. A counterexample must have sums that are genuinely larger than the set of summands but smaller than H.

## 3. Why the generic case resists (recorded obstacle)

Choosing the element 1 in each factor of x(x ⊞ y) and y(x ⊞ y) gives 1 ∈ x^2 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ y^2. Doing it once more gives 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^2y ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy^2 ⊞ y^3. To reach T, the set x^2y ⊞ xy^2 = xy(x ⊞ y) would have to be replaced by its element xy, which is contraction, not containment. This is the same obstacle as (B6) and (B8). The hypothesis a ⊞ -a = H does not help in the generic case, because then no opposite pair occurs among the summands.

## Status

- **Proved:** Lemma 1 and the list of coincidences that make T = H in the class a ⊞ -a = H. Also that the union-type hyperfields of Section 2 (a hyperfield for every G with -1 ≠ 1) satisfy the implication.
- **Open:** the generic case of the class a ⊞ -a = H with -1 ≠ 1. That is: x, y with 1 ∈ x ⊞ y and none of x^3 = -y^3, x^3 = 1, y^3 = 1, xy = 1, y = -x^2, x = -y^2.
- **Open:** part (ii). No counterexample with -1 ≠ 1 was constructed, and no candidate was verified. The headline question remains open.

Background (results obtained earlier in this attempt; each was proved in full in an earlier report, but re-check anything you rely on):

(B1) Conventions. A hyperfield is H = G ∪ {0}, G an abelian multiplicative group, with a commutative, associative multivalued addition ⊞ (sums of several terms are unions over all choices, well defined by associativity), 0 neutral, each a has a unique -a with 0 ∈ a ⊞ -a, reversibility (c ∈ a ⊞ b ⇒ a ∈ c ⊞ -b), and distributivity w(a ⊞ b) = wa ⊞ wb for single elements w. -a = (-1)a with (-1)^2 = 1; possibly -1 = 1. Useful: 0 ∈ A ⊞ B iff A ∩ (-B) ≠ ∅; if c ∈ p ⊞ q then (S ⊞ p ⊞ q) ⊇ (S ⊞ c) ("merging two summands into an element of their sum only shrinks the sum"); H ⊞ a = H for every a; if 0 ∈ S then A ⊞ S ⊇ A.

(B2) Normalization. z = 0 is trivial (y = -x, and 0 ∈ x^3 ⊞ -x^3). For z ≠ 0, scaling by -1/z makes the question equivalent to: for nonzero x, y with 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, is 1 ∈ T := x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ?

(B3) Quotient hyperfields F/U (F a field, U ≤ F^×) satisfy the implication (lift to representatives x'+y'+z' = 0 and use x'^3+y'^3+z'^3-3x'y'z' = (x'+y'+z')(…) = 0). So Krasner, sign, tropical, phase, triangle, weak sign, and all their ordered-group extensions satisfy it; a counterexample must be a NON-quotient hyperfield. Also: if H satisfies it, so does any extension H ⋊ Γ by an ordered abelian group (leading-term argument).

(B4) Computer evidence (exhaustive search, unrefereed): no counterexample among all hyperfields H = G ∪ {0} with |G| ≤ 9 (every abelian group of order ≤ 8, and Z9, Z3×Z3). A counterexample has at least 11 elements.

(B5) Composition rule (proved). If 0 ∈ A ⊞ t and 0 ∈ B ⊞ (-t) for sums A, B and an element t, then 0 ∈ A ⊞ B. (From 0 ∈ A ⊞ t, -t ∈ A; from the other, t ∈ B; and 0 ∈ (-t) ⊞ t.) But from 0 ∈ C ⊞ a ⊞ (-a) one can NOT conclude 0 ∈ C in general.

(B6) Obstruction to "linear" proofs (proved). Treat x, y as formal monomials and let R_w be the relation 0 ∈ wx ⊞ wy ⊞ (-w) (w a monomial ±x^i y^j). No derivation that only composes relations R_w via (B5) yields 0 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ (-1): term counting forces exactly 4 relations, three of which must be R_1, R_{x^2}, R_{y^2}, and the fourth cannot cancel the 6 unwanted terms. The field identity needs the step x^2y + xy^2 = xy, i.e. contracting the SET x^2y ⊞ xy^2 to its element xy, which hyperfield membership does not allow. So an affirmative proof must use auxiliary witness elements (e.g. elements of 1 ⊞ 1, x ⊞ -xy, …) and the associativity/reversibility relations they satisfy.

(B7) Diagonal case (proved). If 1 ∈ x ⊞ x then 1 ∈ T: x^2 ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^3 gives T ⊇ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2, and x ∈ x^2 ⊞ x^2 gives this ⊇ x ⊞ x ∋ 1.

(B8) Expansion with a witness (proved). From 1 ∈ x ⊞ y: x ∈ x^2 ⊞ xy, x^2 ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^2y, so x ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^2y ⊞ xy; similarly y ∈ y^3 ⊞ xy^2 ⊞ xy; hence 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ w for some w ∈ x^2y ⊞ xy^2 = xy(x ⊞ y). So 1 ∈ T whenever this w can be taken to be xy (e.g. whenever x ⊞ y = {1}). In general the witness u ∈ x ⊞ y with w = xy·u need not be 1.

(B9) Class results (proved). (a) If a ⊞ -a = H for all a ≠ 0 and -1 = 1, the implication holds (xy ⊞ xy = H so T = H). With -1 ≠ 1 in this class it is proved only when one of x^3, y^3, z^3 equals xyz; otherwise OPEN. (b) If -1 = 1, then 0 ∈ xy ⊞ xy, so T ⊇ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy, and the implication follows from the core claim (C): 1 ∈ x ⊞ y ⇒ 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy. If a ⊞ a = {a} for all a, then xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy = {xy} and the implication is EQUIVALENT to (C). (C) is OPEN; a field-of-characteristic-2 proof of it uses (x+y)^2 = x^2 + y^2, a cancellation unavailable in hyperfields. (c) Krasner extensions (-1 = 1, a ⊞ a = {0, a}): T = (x^3 ⊞ y^3) ∪ (x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy). These correspond to projective geometries with a regular abelian collineation group; all known ones are quotients (Desarguesian), so they are not promising for a counterexample. (d) Hyperfields in which a ∈ a ⊞ b for all a, b (every multi-sum contains each of its summands), e.g. Massouros' "a ⊞ b = {a, b, a+b} for b ≠ -a, a ⊞ -a = F" built on a field F, satisfy the implication in the cases checked (if x ⊞ y ∋ 1 because 1 ∈ {x, y} then T contains the cube 1; otherwise the field sum 1 = x^3+y^3+3xy is in T).

(B10) Exponent-3 reduction (proved; re-checked independently by three reports). Suppose -1 = 1 and g^3 = 1 for all g ∈ G. Put Q := 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1. Since -1 = 1, y ∈ 1 ⊞ x ⇔ 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, so w := xy ranges over x(1 ⊞ x) = x ⊞ x^2. The normalized target is T = 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ w ⊞ w ⊞ w and 1 ∈ T ⇔ 0 ∈ Q ⊞ wQ ⇔ Q ∩ wQ ≠ ∅. Hence such an H is a counterexample iff there are x ∈ G and nonzero w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with Q ∩ wQ = ∅. This needs 1 ∉ 1 ⊞ 1 (else 0 ∈ Q) and w ≠ 1.

(B11) Further facts in the case -1 = 1 (proved). (a) 1 ∈ Q := 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1 (since 0 ∈ 1 ⊞ 1, Q ⊇ 1 ⊞ 0). (b) Hence in the exponent-3 class of (B10) a counterexample needs x and w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with w ∉ Q and w^{-1} ∉ Q (if w ∈ Q then w = w·1 ∈ Q ∩ wQ; if w^{-1} ∈ Q then 1 = w·w^{-1} ∈ Q ∩ wQ), besides 1 ∉ 1 ⊞ 1, w ≠ 1 and Q ∩ wQ = ∅. (c) Four-point form of associativity: for a commutative hyperaddition with -1 = 1 satisfying reversibility, e ∈ (a ⊞ b) ⊞ c ⇔ (a ⊞ b) ∩ (c ⊞ e) ≠ ∅, so associativity is EQUIVALENT to: for all a, b, c, e ∈ H, (a ⊞ b) ∩ (c ⊞ e) ≠ ∅ ⇔ (b ⊞ c) ∩ (a ⊞ e) ≠ ∅ (i.e. "0 ∈ a ⊞ b ⊞ c ⊞ e" is a symmetric 4-ary relation). The structure is the same as a G-invariant S_3-symmetric set of "triangles" {a, b, c} (0 ∈ a ⊞ b ⊞ c) with the 4-point condition. (d) If moreover 1 ⊞ 1 = {0}, then H is a field: taking a = b in (c), (a ⊞ c) ∩ (a ⊞ e) ≠ ∅ ⇔ c = e, so for fixed a the |H| nonempty sets a ⊞ c (c ∈ H) are pairwise disjoint and cover H (d ∈ a ⊞ c for any c ∈ a ⊞ d), hence all singletons. So in a non-field with -1 = 1, D := (1 ⊞ 1) \ {0} is nonempty, and Q = {1} ∪ (1 ⊞ D) is never just {1}.

(B12) Idempotent class (a ⊞ a = {a} for all a) (proved): with 1 ∈ x ⊞ y one gets 1 ∈ x^2 ⊞ xy ⊞ y^2 (substitute x ∈ x^2 ⊞ xy, y ∈ xy ⊞ y^2 into 1 ∈ x ⊞ y and merge xy ⊞ xy = {xy}) and 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ x^2y ⊞ xy^2 (same again). The target (C) differs only by having the single element xy in place of the set xy(x ⊞ y) ∋ xy; contraction is not allowed.

(B13) Further reductions (proved, elementary). (a) If a hyperfield satisfies the implication, so does every quotient H/U by a subgroup U ≤ G (lift and apply it in H). So a counterexample can be sought "upstairs" in a larger hyperfield. (b) If x ⊞ y = {1}, or one of x, y equals 1, or y = x, the normalized claim holds. # round1_q1: attempt at an affirmative proof. Result: no proof; a structural obstruction is proved

**Status.** I did not settle the question either way. What I did prove is that one natural kind of proof cannot work: a proof that only combines multiples of the hypothesis relation by cancelling one term at a time. Any affirmative proof therefore has to bring in more of the hyperfield structure. I did not construct a counterexample either.

Normalized form, from (B2) of the task file: from 1 ∈ x⊞y, conclude 1 ∈ x³⊞y³⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy. Equivalently, 0 ∈ x³⊞y³⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy⊞(−1).

## 1. The composition rule (proved)

Here A and B are hypersums of finitely many terms, and t is an element.

**Rule.** If 0 ∈ A⊞t and 0 ∈ B⊞(−t), then 0 ∈ A⊞B.

*Proof.*
1. From 0 ∈ A⊞t there is an a ∈ A with 0 ∈ a⊞t. By uniqueness of negatives, a = −t, so −t ∈ A.
2. In the same way, from 0 ∈ B⊞(−t) we get t ∈ B.
3. Since 0 ∈ (−t)⊞t, it follows that 0 ∈ A⊞B. ∎

There is also a weakening step: 0 ∈ C⊞a⊞(−a) holds for every element a and every sum C, so it carries no information.

**What the rule does not give.** You cannot cancel a pair a, −a that sits inside a single relation: from 0 ∈ C⊞a⊞(−a) you cannot conclude 0 ∈ C. This is exactly where the field proof breaks down.

## 2. Obstruction for "linear" proofs (proved)

**Admissible derivations.** Call a derivation admissible if it uses only:
- the relations R_w : 0 ∈ wx⊞wy⊞(−w), for monomials w = ±xⁱyʲ (these come from distributivity applied to 0 ∈ x⊞y⊞(−1));
- the composition rule of §1.

**Term count.** Composing k such relations needs k−1 cancellations. Each cancellation removes 2 terms, so the result has 3k − 2(k−1) = k+2 terms, counted with multiplicity.

**Claim.** The target relation 0 ∈ x³⊞y³⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy⊞(−1) has 6 terms, so an admissible derivation would need exactly k = 4 relations. Taking x, y to be formal monomials, no choice of 4 relations works.

*Proof.* Treat x, y as formal monomials, i.e. as independent indeterminates with no relations among their monomials.
1. **Which relations are forced.**
   - The term −1 can only come from R_1. Its terms are x, y, −1.
   - The term x³ can only come from R_{x²}. Its terms are x³, x²y, −x².
   - The term y³ can only come from R_{y²}. Its terms are xy², y³, −y².
2. **No cancellation among these three.** None of the nine terms of R_1, R_{x²}, R_{y²} is the negative of another of them, formally.
3. **The fourth relation is too small.** The single remaining relation would therefore have to supply all 3 cancellations, one for each of its 3 terms. That would remove 3 of the 6 unwanted terms x, y, x²y, −x², xy², −y².
4. **Conclusion.** At least 3 unwanted terms survive, and no xy term is produced at all. So no admissible derivation exists. ∎

**Consequence.** The field identity has no "tree-shaped" realization.
- A natural field derivation uses x² = x − xy and x³ = x − xy − x²y, and then the step x²y + xy² = xy.
- That last step needs the *set* x²y⊞xy² to be contracted to its element xy.
- Hyperfield membership only allows replacing an element by a set that contains it, never contracting a set to one of its elements.

Any affirmative proof must therefore use extra elements of H: auxiliary witnesses c taken from sums such as 1⊞1 or x⊞(−xy), together with relations satisfied by those witnesses. Arbitrary hyperfields need not have such relations. This, together with (B3), is evidence that the answer may be NO. It is only evidence, and it conflicts with the unrefereed computer search reported in (B5).

## 3. Proved positive cases (taken from the task background, rechecked)

- **z = 0.** Then 0 ∈ x⊞y forces y = −x, and the target set x³⊞(−x³) contains 0.
- **Quotient hyperfields F/U.** Choose representatives x', y', z' of the classes with x'+y'+z' = 0. Then x'³+y'³+z'³−3x'y'z' = 0 in F. Since x'³ ∈ [x]³ and x'y'z' ∈ [xyz], the class of 0 lies in the target sum.

## Open

- The main question is still open.
- The concrete open sub-problem is to find a hyperfield in which no auxiliary witnesses rescue the conclusion. Such a hyperfield would be a counterexample.
- One approach is a "freely generated" non-quotient hyperfield, in which hypersums are as small as the axioms allow around the relation 1 ∈ x⊞y. I did not build or verify such an object.

=== END OF ANSWER round1_q1 ===
# round1_q3 — partial answer (question not settled)

**Status:** I found neither a proof nor a counterexample. Below are the proved results, followed by the exact remaining obstacle.

I use the normalized form (B2): given 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, is 1 ∈ T := x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy?

## Basic tool (proved)
If a ∈ S (a hypersum) then any multi-sum containing a as one summand is contained in the same multi-sum with S in place of a. This holds by associativity and because sums are unions over choices. It follows that replacing one summand c by a set that contains c can only shrink the target. That is the wrong direction for a proof, but it is used below in the following form: if c ∈ (p ⊞ q), then (… ⊞ p ⊞ q) ⊇ (… ⊞ c).

## Proposition 1 (diagonal case, proved): if 1 ∈ x ⊞ x, then 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^3 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2.
Proof.
1. Multiplying 1 ∈ x ⊞ x by x^2 gives x^2 ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^3.
2. Therefore x^3 ⊞ x^3 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊇ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2, choosing x^2 from x^3 ⊞ x^3.
3. Multiplying by x gives x ∈ x^2 ⊞ x^2, so x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊇ x ⊞ x.
4. Since 1 ∈ x ⊞ x, the target contains 1. ∎

## Proposition 2 (expansion, proved): 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ w for some w ∈ xy(x ⊞ y).
Proof.
1. From 1 ∈ x ⊞ y we get x ∈ x^2 ⊞ xy and x^2 ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^2y, so x ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^2y ⊞ xy.
2. Similarly y ∈ y^3 ⊞ xy^2 ⊞ xy.
3. Hence 1 ∈ x ⊞ y ⊆ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ (x^2y ⊞ xy^2), and x^2y ⊞ xy^2 = xy(x ⊞ y). ∎

So the implication holds whenever this witness can be taken to be w = xy, i.e. whenever the element u ∈ x ⊞ y used here can be taken to be 1. In particular it holds whenever x ⊞ y = {1}. For example, this covers hyperfields in which x ⊞ y is a singleton for this pair.

## Remaining obstacle (open)
In general the witness u ∈ x ⊞ y produced by the associativity bracketing need not equal 1. The field proof uses cancellation in the factorisation x^3 + y^3 + 3xy − 1 = (x + y − 1)(x^2 − xy + y^2 + x + y + 1). In a hyperfield, a ⊞ −a may be strictly larger than {0}, so that cancellation is not available.

- A counterexample would have to be a hyperfield that is not a quotient of a field (B3).
- By the run's search (B5), it would also have to be larger than every case covered there: |G| ≤ 8 and G = Z3 × Z3.
- I did not build or analyze the free "closure" hyperfield suggested in the task.

**The question remains open:** is 1 ∈ T forced in every hyperfield (equivalently, can the witness u in Proposition 2 always be taken to be 1)?

=== END OF ANSWER round1_q3 ===

## Lemma 0 (absorption). For any a, H ⊞ a = H. Also, if S ∋ 0 then A ⊞ S ⊇ A for any set A.
Proof. Given c, pick h ∈ c⊞-a (this set is nonempty). By reversibility c ∈ h⊞a. The second claim holds because A⊞S ⊇ A⊞0 = A. ∎

## (v) Hyperfields with a⊞-a = H for all a ≠ 0: the implication holds. (Proved.)
Normalize so that x, y ≠ 0. Case -1 = 1: then xy⊞xy = xy⊞-xy = H, so T ⊇ x³⊞y³⊞xy⊞H = H by Lemma 0, and 1 ∈ T. Case -1 ≠ 1: work in the unnormalized form. The target contains x³ ⊞ (-xyz ⊞ ...). If z = 0 the claim is trivial by (B2). Otherwise, if x³ = xyz then x³ ⊞ -xyz = H, so the target is H ⊞ (rest) = H, by Lemma 0. In general this argument needs one of x³, y³, z³ to equal xyz. So for (v) with -1 ≠ 1 only that special case is proved, and the rest is open. The hypothesis "a⊞-a ⊇ {0,a,-a}" gives nothing beyond this by the same method.

 (C) 1 ∈ x⊞y ⇒ 1 ∈ x³⊞y³⊞xy.
Proof. In the second case, T = (x³⊞y³⊞xy)⊞(xy⊞xy) ⊇ x³⊞y³⊞xy by Lemma 0. The first case is analogous, with core x³⊞y³ (stronger). ∎

- (ii) If a⊞a = {a}, then xy⊞xy⊞xy = {xy}, so T = x³⊞y³⊞xy exactly, and the problem is equivalent to (C).
Restatement of (C): (x³⊞y³) ∩ (1⊞-xy) ≠ ∅. I could not prove (C) and found no counterexample to it. In a field of characteristic 2, x³+y³ = (x+y)(x²+xy+y²) = x²+xy+y² = 1+xy uses cancellation (x+y)² = x²+y², which is not available in a hyperfield (1 ∈ x⊞y gives only 1 ∈ x²⊞xy⊞xy⊞y²).

From memory (Bowler–Su): every stringent hyperfield is isomorphic to a field, to K or S, or to an extension of one of these by an ordered abelian group (H ⋊ Γ). I believe each of these is a quotient F/U of a field: take Hahn series k((Γ)) modulo 1+𝔪, and then also modulo the residue units or the squares for K and S. Given this, (B3) applies and the implication holds. This step is cited from memory and not re-verified.

## (iv) Doubly distributive hyperfields. Conditional on a cited result.
From memory, Bowler–Su also classify these: fields, K, S, W (the weak sign hyperfield) and their extensions by ordered groups. W is a quotient of a finite field by its squares; for example, in F_7 the sum 1+1=2 is a square and 1+2=3 is a nonsquare, giving 1⊞1 = {±1}. - it has at least 10 elements (B5);

# round2_q3: attempt at a counterexample via the exponent-3 route

## What this file contains
I did not find a counterexample, and I did not prove that the exponent-3 route is impossible. Below are a check of (B10), one new proved constraint on any counterexample in that class, and a record of a failed construction.

## 1. Check of (B10) (proved)
Assume -1 = 1 and g^3 = 1 for every g in G. Put x^3 = y^3 = 1 and w = xy. Then T = 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ w ⊞ w ⊞ w. By reversibility (with -1 = 1), 1 ∈ T if and only if 0 ∈ 1⊞1⊞1⊞w⊞w⊞w = Q ⊞ wQ. That holds if and only if Q ∩ (-wQ) = Q ∩ wQ ≠ ∅. Also y ∈ 1 ⊞ x if and only if 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, so w ranges over x ⊞ x^2. So (B10) is correct.

## 2. New constraint (proved)
**Lemma.** If -1 = 1, then 1 ∈ Q = 1⊞1⊞1 always.

*Proof.* 1 ∈ Q if and only if 0 ∈ 1⊞1⊞1⊞1 = (1⊞1) ⊞ (1⊞1). That holds if and only if (1⊞1) ∩ -(1⊞1) = (1⊞1) ∩ (1⊞1) is nonempty, which is true. ∎

**Corollary.** In the exponent-3 class, a counterexample needs x and w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with **w ∉ Q and w^{-1} = w^2 ∉ Q**.
- If w ∈ Q, then w = w·1 ∈ wQ (by the Lemma), so w ∈ Q ∩ wQ.
- If w^{-1} ∈ Q, then 1 = w·w^{-1} ∈ wQ and 1 ∈ Q.

Together with (B10), a counterexample in this class also needs 1 ∉ 1 ⊞ 1 and w ≠ 1. In addition, Q must be disjoint from the whole translate wQ. Since 1 ∈ Q, this means wQ must avoid both 1 and w.

## 3. A construction that fails
I wrote G additively as V = F_3^k. The first candidate takes the triangles to be the affine lines {a, b, c} with a+b+c = 0 (a, b, c distinct), together with a ⊞ a = {0}. This addition is single-valued, a ⊞ b = -a-b, and it is **not associative**: (a⊞b)⊞c = a+b-c, but a⊞(b⊞c) = a-b-c.

Adding the degenerate triangles {a, a, c} for c - a in a set D makes a ∈ a ⊞ c. If every sum contains its summands, we are in class (B9d), which cannot give a counterexample. I did not complete an associativity analysis for a partial D.

## Open
- Whether some hyperfield with -1 = 1 and G of exponent 3 has x and w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with Q ∩ wQ = ∅. By the Corollary, it would need w, w^2 ∉ Q.
- The headline question remains open.

=== END OF ANSWER round2_q3 ===
# round2_q1 — answer (partial; core claim not settled)

## Status
I could not prove (C), or the headline implication, for all hyperfields with -1 = 1. I also could not build a counterexample. Below are the checks and the small partial results that I did prove.

## Checks of the background
- (B9)(b) holds. If -1 = 1, then 0 ∈ xy ⊞ xy. So xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊇ xy ⊞ 0 = {xy}, and therefore T ⊇ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy.
- 1 ∈ Q := 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1 always holds when -1 = 1, since 0 ∈ 1 ⊞ 1 gives Q ⊇ 1 ⊞ 0 = {1}.
- (B10) holds. Take g^3 = 1 for all g ∈ G and -1 = 1. Then x^3 = y^3 = 1 and T = 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ wQ, where w = xy. We have 1 ∈ T ⇔ 0 ∈ 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ wQ ⇔ Q ∩ wQ ≠ ∅, because -a = a, so 0 ∈ A ⊞ B ⇔ A ∩ B ≠ ∅. Reversibility gives y ∈ 1 ⊞ x, so w ∈ x ⊞ x^2.

## Partial results (proved)
**P1 (exponent 3, w ∈ Q).** In the setting of (B10), if w ∈ Q or w^{-1} ∈ Q, then 1 ∈ T.
Proof. If w ∈ Q: 1 ∈ Q gives w ∈ wQ, so w ∈ Q ∩ wQ. If w^{-1} ∈ Q: 1 ∈ Q gives w ∈ wQ, and w·w^{-1} = 1 ∈ Q; also 1 ∈ wQ, since 1 = w·w^{-1} with w^{-1} ∈ Q. So 1 ∈ Q ∩ wQ. ∎
So an exponent-3 counterexample needs an x and a w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with w ∉ Q, w^{-1} ∉ Q and Q ∩ wQ = ∅. In particular w ≠ 1, and Q must be a proper subset of H.

**P2.** If x ⊞ y = {1}, the claim holds by (B8). If a ⊞ a = H for all a ≠ 0, it holds by (B9)(a).

## Remaining obstacle (open)
- Main open question: (C) "1 ∈ x ⊞ y ⇒ 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy" when -1 = 1. The weaker target, 1 ∈ T, is also open.

- Counterexample search: in the exponent-3 case, by P1 one should look for 1 ∉ 1 ⊞ 1 with Q small. One should also look for a G-invariant triangle system in which x ⊞ x^2 avoids Q ∪ Q^{-1} and avoids every w with Q ∩ wQ ≠ ∅. This search was not carried out.

# round1_q2: looking for a counterexample (partial result)

**Status: no counterexample found, and the question is still open.** What follows is a few small reductions that are proved, plus an account of the one candidate family I checked, which fails.

Normalized form (B2): we need nonzero x, y with 1 ∈ x⊞y but 1 ∉ T := x^3⊞y^3⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy.

## Lemma 1 (proved): Krasner extensions, i.e. -1 = 1 and a⊞a = {0,a}
In a hyperfield of this kind, xy⊞xy⊞xy = {0,xy}⊞xy = {xy} ∪ {0,xy} = {0,xy}.
So T = (x^3⊞y^3) ∪ (x^3⊞y^3⊞xy). A counterexample therefore needs both 1 ∉ x^3⊞y^3 and 1 ∉ x^3⊞y^3⊞xy.

If x = y, then 1 ∈ {0,x} forces x = 1. In that case T = 1⊞1⊞1⊞1⊞1 ⊇ 0⊞0⊞1 ∋ 1, so the conclusion holds.
Otherwise 1, x, y are three distinct points on one line of the associated geometry. The conclusion then comes down to this: 1 must lie in the hypersum x^3⊞y^3 or in x^3⊞y^3⊞xy. In geometric terms these are roughly the line through x^3, y^3 and the span of x^3, y^3, xy, minus some degenerate points.

## Example 2 (checked): the "one-line" Krasner extension fails
Take H = G ∪ {0} with x⊞y = G \ {x,y} for x ≠ y, and x⊞x = {0,x}. I assume the axioms hold for |G| large enough; I did not re-verify this. Here 1 ∈ x⊞y exactly when 1, x, y are distinct.

- If x^3 ≠ y^3 and 1 ∉ {x^3, y^3}, then 1 ∈ x^3⊞y^3, so the conclusion holds.
- If x^3 = 1 or y^3 = 1, then T contains 1, because we can take 0 from xy⊞xy⊞xy and 0 from the remaining cube's pairing… In detail: if x^3 = 1, choose y^3⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy so that it contains 0. This works because it contains y^3⊞{0,xy}, and that contains 0 when y^3 = xy; otherwise it contains G \ {y^3,xy}, which can be chosen to meet the needed element. This bullet is only sketched.
- In the remaining case x^3 = y^3 = t ≠ 1 with x ≠ y, we get x^3⊞y^3 = {0,t}. So T ⊇ {0,t}⊞xy ⊇ {xy} ∪ (G \ {t,xy}).
  - This avoids 1 only if xy = 1 or t = xy.
  - t = xy means y = x^2, which gives x^6 = x^3, so t = 1, a contradiction.
  - xy = 1 forces x^6 = 1 with x^3 ≠ 1. But then T ⊇ {0,t}⊞(1⊞1⊞1) = {0,t}⊞{0,1} ∋ 1, so the conclusion holds again.

So this family gives no counterexample, apart from the one step sketched in the second bullet. This fits (B3)/(B5): such hyperfields are often quotients anyway.

## What remains open
- The headline question itself.
- Lemma 1 suggests a precise sub-question: for a Krasner extension coming from a geometry with a simply transitive abelian group action, does collinearity of 1, x, y force 1 ∈ (x^3⊞y^3) ∪ (x^3⊞y^3⊞xy)? Non-Desarguesian planes with an abelian Singer-type action would be the natural place to test this. I did not settle it.
- Candidate families (b) and (d) from the task were not examined.

=== END OF ANSWER round1_q2 ===

30	(A1) Conventions. A hyperfield is H = G ∪ {0}, G an abelian multiplicative group, with a commutative, associative multivalued addition ⊞ (sums of several terms are unions over all choices, well defined by associativity), 0 neutral, each a has a unique -a with 0 ∈ a ⊞ -a, reversibility (c ∈ a ⊞ b ⇒ a ∈ c ⊞ -b), and distributivity w(a ⊞ b) = wa ⊞ wb for single elements w. -a = (-1)a with (-1)^2 = 1; possibly -1 = 1. 49	**Rule.** If 0 ∈ A⊞t and 0 ∈ B⊞(−t), then 0 ∈ A⊞B.

62	**Admissible derivations.** Call a derivation admissible if it uses only:
63	- the relations R_w : 0 ∈ wx⊞wy⊞(−w), for monomials w = ±xⁱyʲ (these come from distributivity applied to 0 ∈ x⊞y⊞(−1));

66	**Term count.** Composing k such relations needs k−1 cancellations. Each cancellation removes 2 terms, so the result has 3k − 2(k−1) = k+2 terms, counted with multiplicity.

68	**Claim.** The target relation 0 ∈ x³⊞y³⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy⊞(−1) has 6 terms, so an admissible derivation would need exactly k = 4 relations. Taking x, y to be formal monomials, no choice of 4 relations works.

73	   - The term x³ can only come from R_{x²}. Its terms are x³, x²y, −x².

165	## 2. Linear derivations fail in the exponent-3 class (proved)
166	
167	**Admissible moves.** Only the following moves are allowed:
168	- the relations 0 ∈ mx ⊞ mx² ⊞ mw, for monomials m = x^i w^j;
169	- the pairs 0 ∈ a⊞a;
170	- disjoint union of zero-sums (if 0 ∈ A and 0 ∈ B then 0 ∈ A⊞B);
171	- composition (B5), which cancels one shared term between two different components.
172	
173	Cancelling a term inside a single component is not allowed (see B5).
174	
175	**Claim.** In the generic situation, where the 9 monomials x^i w^j are distinct, no such derivation produces 0 ∈ 1⊞1⊞1⊞w⊞w⊞w. (Specific Δ might create extra coincidences among the monomials; that case is not covered.)
176	
177	**Proof.**
178	
179	*Step 1 (counting).* A component built from n triangles linked in a tree has n+2 remaining terms. A pair component has 2 terms. Attaching a pair to an existing term changes nothing, because 0∈A⊞a together with 0∈a⊞a gives back 0∈A⊞a. To get 6 terms, the possible shapes are:
180	- (i) a single tree of 4 triangles;
181	- (ii) a tree of 2 triangles plus one pair;
182	- (iii) two separate triangles.
183	
184	*Step 2 (shapes (ii) and (iii)).* Each triangle has 3 distinct terms. Shape (ii) would need three equal leftover terms from two triangles; shape (iii) would need a triangle {1,1,w} or {1,w,w}. Both are impossible.
185	
186	*Step 3 (shape (i), reduction to the group ring).* Reduce mod 2 in R = F_2[x,w]/(x³−1, w³−1) ≅ (F_2 × F_4)⊗(F_2 × F_4). Let f be the sum of the four chosen m's. Then f·(x+x²+w) = 1+w + 2(cancelled pairs) ≡ 1+w.
187	
188	*Step 4 (solving at x = 1).* At x = 1 we have x+x² = 0. The equation becomes f(1,w)·w = 1+w, so f(1,w) = 1+w².
189	
190	*Step 5 (solving at x = ω).* At x = ω we have x+x² = 1. The equation becomes f(ω,w)(1+w) = 1+w, so f(ω,w) ≡ 1 mod (1+w+w²).
191	
192	*Step 6 (all solutions).* Write f = a + b w + c w². The conditions give a = 1, b = 0, c = 1+x+x², up to the kernel, which is h(x)(1+w+w²) with h ∈ {0, x+x², 1+x, 1+x²}. So the solutions are
193	
194	f = 1 + (1+x+x²)w² + h(x)(1+w+w²).
195	
196	The 4-term solutions include:
197	- {1, w², xw², x²w²};
198	- x + (1+x)w + x²w², i.e. {x, w, xw, x²w²}.
199	
200	*Step 7 (checking multiplicities).* Expand the integer multiset of terms for either 4-term solution. It contains 1 and w exactly once each, and five other monomials exactly twice each. 287	- on F_3^3, among systems invariant under multiplication by the order-13 subgroup of F_27^*;
288	- on F_3^4, among systems invariant under multiplication by F_81^*.
289	
290	In every non-field associative system the coordinator enumerated with 1 ∉ 1⊞1 (F_3^2 and F_3^3 with various multiplicative symmetries), Q = 1⊞1⊞1 contained all of G, so the claim held trivially. Any counterexample in this class must live on a larger group F_3^k (k ≥ 5, or infinite rank) and have small sums.
291	
292	(C3) Krasner extensions (-1 = 1 and a⊞a = {0, a}) correspond to projective geometries with point set G, on which G acts regularly by multiplication; here a⊞b is the line through a and b with a and b removed, for a ≠ b. In this class the claim becomes an incidence statement. All known such geometries are Desarguesian, hence quotients, hence satisfy the claim. So this class was judged unpromising, but it has not been refuted as a source of counterexamples.
293	
294	(C4) Free-hyperfield reformulation (coordinator's observation, not refereed). Build a hyperfield "freely" from generators x, y and the single relation 1 ∈ x⊞y, by a chase: repeatedly add every membership forced by distributivity, commutativity and reversibility, and for every associativity instance and every empty sum add a fresh group generator as witness. If the resulting limit is a hyperfield (a statement still to be checked), then it maps to every hyperfield containing such x, y by a membership-preserving map. The question is then equivalent to whether 1 ∈ T holds in this free object. A counterexample amounts to an invariant of the chase steps that the target violates.
295	
296	## The coordinator's sketch (a suggestion only; you may discard it)
297	Why it should hold (coordinator's sketch; I am genuinely unsure of the truth value).
298	- For: (C1) shows no counterexample below 11 elements. (C2) shows that in the exponent-3 char-2 class every small structure has Q = G. Every structured family examined satisfies N: quotients, union-type, a⊞-a = H with -1 = 1, circular/ordered types (an informal check by the coordinator: 1 lies "between" x and y, so 1 lies in the cone of x^3, y^3, xy).
299	- A proof must use witnesses: linear derivations fail (#2, round3_q1, round3_q2). Candidate mechanism: the zero-sum calculus. Its moves are composition along a shared element, splitting a zero-sum Z = Z1 ⊔ Z2 into Z1+t, Z2+(-t) with a fresh t (this is associativity), scaling, and adding pairs {a, -a}. The field identity 1 - x^3 - y^3 - 3xy = (1 - x - y)(1 + x + y + x^2 - xy + y^2) needs the six scaled hypothesis relations R_m (m ∈ {1, x, y, x^2, -xy, y^2}). Their 18 terms cancel in 6 opposite pairs, but a tree of 6 relations allows only 5 gluings, so one cycle remains (for (C) with -1 = 1, 7 cancellations are needed against 5 gluings). The hope is that splitting closes the extra cycle(s), by routing them through fresh witnesses that are then eliminated by composing two copies of a split.
300	- Against: the free hyperfield of (C4). If the chase never needs the cycle-closing step, the free object is a counterexample. Showing that needs an invariant of chase steps, e.g. a weight on fresh generators, that the target violates.
301	
302	
303	## What to return
304	Start with a one-line verdict: PROVED (N), COUNTEREXAMPLE to (N), or PARTIAL. Then give the full argument. Every step must be checkable from the hyperfield axioms. For a proof, state every auxiliary element you introduce and the axiom that produces it. For a counterexample, give the full structure and the full axiom verification.

28	## Part A. Conventions and coordinator facts
29	
30	(A1) Conventions. A hyperfield is H = G ∪ {0}, G an abelian multiplicative group, with a commutative, associative multivalued addition ⊞ (sums of several terms are unions over all choices, well defined by associativity), 0 neutral, each a has a unique -a with 0 ∈ a ⊞ -a, reversibility (c ∈ a ⊞ b ⇒ a ∈ c ⊞ -b), and distributivity w(a ⊞ b) = wa ⊞ wb for single elements w. -a = (-1)a with (-1)^2 = 1; possibly -1 = 1. Useful: 0 ∈ A ⊞ B iff A ∩ (-B) ≠ ∅; if c ∈ p ⊞ q then (S ⊞ p ⊞ q) ⊇ (S ⊞ c) ("merging two summands into an element of their sum only shrinks the sum"); H ⊞ a = H for every a; if 0 ∈ S then A ⊞ S ⊇ A.
31	
32	(A2) Normalization. z = 0 is trivial (y = -x, and 0 ∈ x^3 ⊞ -x^3). For z ≠ 0, scaling by -1/z makes the question equivalent to: for nonzero x, y with 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, is 1 ∈ T := x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ?
33	
34	(A3) Quotient hyperfields F/U (F a field, U ≤ F^×) satisfy the implication (lift to representatives x'+y'+z' = 0 and use x'^3+y'^3+z'^3-3x'y'z' = (x'+y'+z')(…) = 0). So Krasner, sign, tropical, phase, triangle, weak sign, and all their ordered-group extensions satisfy it; a counterexample must be a NON-quotient hyperfield. Also: if H satisfies it, so does any extension H ⋊ Γ by an ordered abelian group (leading-term argument).
35	
36	(A4) [old label B10] Exponent-3 reduction (proved; re-checked independently by three reports). Suppose -1 = 1 and g^3 = 1 for all g ∈ G. Put Q := 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1. Since -1 = 1, y ∈ 1 ⊞ x ⇔ 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, so w := xy ranges over x(1 ⊞ x) = x ⊞ x^2. The normalized target is T = 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ w ⊞ w ⊞ w and 1 ∈ T ⇔ 0 ∈ Q ⊞ wQ ⇔ Q ∩ wQ ≠ ∅. Hence such an H is a counterexample iff there are x ∈ G and nonzero w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with Q ∩ wQ = ∅. This needs 1 ∉ 1 ⊞ 1 (else 0 ∈ Q) and w ≠ 1.
37	
38	(A5) [old label B11] Further facts in the case -1 = 1 (proved). (a) 1 ∈ Q := 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1 (since 0 ∈ 1 ⊞ 1, Q ⊇ 1 ⊞ 0). (b) Hence in the exponent-3 class of (B10) a counterexample needs x and w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with w ∉ Q and w^{-1} ∉ Q (if w ∈ Q then w = w·1 ∈ Q ∩ wQ; if w^{-1} ∈ Q then 1 = w·w^{-1} ∈ Q ∩ wQ), besides 1 ∉ 1 ⊞ 1, w ≠ 1 and Q ∩ wQ = ∅. (c) Four-point form of associativity: for a commutative hyperaddition with -1 = 1 satisfying reversibility, e ∈ (a ⊞ b) ⊞ c ⇔ (a ⊞ b) ∩ (c ⊞ e) ≠ ∅, so associativity is EQUIVALENT to: for all a, b, c, e ∈ H, (a ⊞ b) ∩ (c ⊞ e) ≠ ∅ ⇔ (b ⊞ c) ∩ (a ⊞ e) ≠ ∅ (i.e. "0 ∈ a ⊞ b ⊞ c ⊞ e" is a symmetric 4-ary relation).
