36	## Part A. Conventions and coordinator facts
37	
38	(A1) Conventions. A hyperfield is H = G ∪ {0}, G an abelian multiplicative group, with a commutative, associative multivalued addition ⊞ (sums of several terms are unions over all choices, well defined by associativity), 0 neutral, each a has a unique -a with 0 ∈ a ⊞ -a, reversibility (c ∈ a ⊞ b ⇒ a ∈ c ⊞ -b), and distributivity w(a ⊞ b) = wa ⊞ wb for single elements w. -a = (-1)a with (-1)^2 = 1; possibly -1 = 1. Useful: 0 ∈ A ⊞ B iff A ∩ (-B) ≠ ∅; if c ∈ p ⊞ q then (S ⊞ p ⊞ q) ⊇ (S ⊞ c) ("merging two summands into an element of their sum only shrinks the sum"); H ⊞ a = H for every a; if 0 ∈ S then A ⊞ S ⊇ A.
39	
40	(A2) Normalization. z = 0 is trivial (y = -x, and 0 ∈ x^3 ⊞ -x^3). For z ≠ 0, scaling by -1/z makes the question equivalent to: for nonzero x, y with 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, is 1 ∈ T := x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ?
41	
42	(A3) Quotient hyperfields F/U (F a field, U ≤ F^×) satisfy the implication (lift to representatives x'+y'+z' = 0 and use x'^3+y'^3+z'^3-3x'y'z' = (x'+y'+z')(…) = 0). So Krasner, sign, tropical, phase, triangle, weak sign, and all their ordered-group extensions satisfy it; a counterexample must be a NON-quotient hyperfield. Also: if H satisfies it, so does any extension H ⋊ Γ by an ordered abelian group (leading-term argument).
43	
44	(A4) [old label B10] Exponent-3 reduction (proved; re-checked independently by three reports). Suppose -1 = 1 and g^3 = 1 for all g ∈ G. Put Q := 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1. Since -1 = 1, y ∈ 1 ⊞ x ⇔ 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, so w := xy ranges over x(1 ⊞ x) = x ⊞ x^2. The normalized target is T = 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ w ⊞ w ⊞ w and 1 ∈ T ⇔ 0 ∈ Q ⊞ wQ ⇔ Q ∩ wQ ≠ ∅. Hence such an H is a counterexample iff there are x ∈ G and nonzero w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with Q ∩ wQ = ∅. This needs 1 ∉ 1 ⊞ 1 (else 0 ∈ Q) and w ≠ 1.

2	
3	Open question attempted: the problem's claim within the class of hyperfields with -1 ≠ 1 and a⊞-a = H for every a ≠ 0. This is an open gap of this attempt: the generic case in that class is unresolved. It is equivalent to the statement (N) restricted to that class. (N) is stated here:
4	
5	Missing statement (N). Let H be a hyperfield: H = G ∪ {0}, where G is an abelian multiplicative group, and ⊞ is a commutative, associative multivalued addition with nonempty values, with 0 neutral, a unique -a for each a with 0 ∈ a⊞-a, reversibility (c ∈ a⊞b ⇒ a ∈ c⊞-b), and distributivity w(a⊞b) = wa⊞wb. Let x, y ∈ G with 1 ∈ x⊞y. Then 1 ∈ T := x^3⊞y^3⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy.
6	
7	(N) is equivalent to the problem's question: if z = 0 the claim is trivial; otherwise scale by -z^{-1}. A COUNTEREXAMPLE in this class answers the whole problem "no". A proof for this class alone settles only a sub-case, though it would still be worth having.
8	
9	What is known in this class (background B-7 and B-3 below):
10	- Any multi-sum with two opposite nonzero summands equals H. So (N) holds whenever x^3 = -y^3, x^3 = 1, y^3 = 1, xy = 1, y = -x^2, or x = -y^2.
11	- The union-type hyperfields (a⊞b = {a, b} for b ≠ -a) satisfy (N).
12	- A counterexample must have sums a⊞b, for b ≠ -a, that are strictly bigger than {a, b} but are not H.
13	
14	Generic case: x, y nonzero with 1 ∈ x⊞y, none of the coincidences above, and xy⊞xy ∌ 0.
15	
16	Task. Either
17	(a) construct a hyperfield in this class that violates (N) in the generic case, with every axiom verified (associativity for all triples), or
18	(b) prove (N) for the whole class.
19	
20	Hints you may discard:
21	- In this class, (a⊞b)⊞c = H as soon as -c ∈ a⊞b. So associativity strongly constrains which "middle-sized" sums are possible.
22	- Try first to classify the possible sum-rules. For example: on G = Z/n × {±1}, or on G = (circle group) × {±1}, with a⊞b determined by a "distance" between a and b. Then test (N) on each.
23	- Also consider whether a hyperfield in this class can be built from any hyperfield K with -1 ≠ 1 by "enlarging" a⊞-a to all of H. Determine when that preserves associativity, and whether it can destroy (N).
24	
25	Do not report "this is open" as a result.
26	
27	BACKGROUND: results obtained so far in this attempt
28	
29	Part A collects conventions and coordinator facts. Part B reproduces verbatim the proved parts of earlier reports, with their proofs. Labels such as (B3), (B5), (B10), (B11c) inside the reproduced passages refer to background lists that those reports were given. Wherever such a label matters, its content is restated in Part A (A1 = old B1, A2 = old B2, A3 = old B3, A4 = old B10, A5 = old B11). Otherwise ignore it. Part C gives unrefereed computational evidence and the coordinator's observations. Re-check anything you rely on.
30	
31	## Part A. Conventions and coordinator facts
32	
33	(A1) Conventions. A hyperfield is H = G ∪ {0}, G an abelian multiplicative group, with a commutative, associative multivalued addition ⊞ (sums of several terms are unions over all choices, well defined by associativity), 0 neutral, each a has a unique -a with 0 ∈ a ⊞ -a, reversibility (c ∈ a ⊞ b ⇒ a ∈ c ⊞ -b), and distributivity w(a ⊞ b) = wa ⊞ wb for single elements w. -a = (-1)a with (-1)^2 = 1; possibly -1 = 1. Useful: 0 ∈ A ⊞ B iff A ∩ (-B) ≠ ∅; if c ∈ p ⊞ q then (S ⊞ p ⊞ q) ⊇ (S ⊞ c) ("merging two summands into an element of their sum only shrinks the sum"); H ⊞ a = H for every a; if 0 ∈ S then A ⊞ S ⊇ A.
34	
35	(A2) Normalization. z = 0 is trivial (y = -x, and 0 ∈ x^3 ⊞ -x^3). For z ≠ 0, scaling by -1/z makes the question equivalent to: for nonzero x, y with 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, is 1 ∈ T := x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ?
36	
37	(A3) Quotient hyperfields F/U (F a field, U ≤ F^×) satisfy the implication (lift to representatives x'+y'+z' = 0 and use x'^3+y'^3+z'^3-3x'y'z' = (x'+y'+z')(…) = 0). So Krasner, sign, tropical, phase, triangle, weak sign, and all their ordered-group extensions satisfy it; a counterexample must be a NON-quotient hyperfield. Also: if H satisfies it, so does any extension H ⋊ Γ by an ordered abelian group (leading-term argument).
38	
39	(A4) [old label B10] Exponent-3 reduction (proved; re-checked independently by three reports). Suppose -1 = 1 and g^3 = 1 for all g ∈ G. Put Q := 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1. Since -1 = 1, y ∈ 1 ⊞ x ⇔ 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, so w := xy ranges over x(1 ⊞ x) = x ⊞ x^2. The normalized target is T = 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ w ⊞ w ⊞ w and 1 ∈ T ⇔ 0 ∈ Q ⊞ wQ ⇔ Q ∩ wQ ≠ ∅. Hence such an H is a counterexample iff there are x ∈ G and nonzero w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with Q ∩ wQ = ∅. This needs 1 ∉ 1 ⊞ 1 (else 0 ∈ Q) and w ≠ 1.
40	
41	(A5) [old label B11] Further facts in the case -1 = 1 (proved). (a) 1 ∈ Q := 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ 1 (since 0 ∈ 1 ⊞ 1, Q ⊇ 1 ⊞ 0). (b) Hence in the exponent-3 class of (B10) a counterexample needs x and w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with w ∉ Q and w^{-1} ∉ Q (if w ∈ Q then w = w·1 ∈ Q ∩ wQ; if w^{-1} ∈ Q then 1 = w·w^{-1} ∈ Q ∩ wQ), besides 1 ∉ 1 ⊞ 1, w ≠ 1 and Q ∩ wQ = ∅. (c) Four-point form of associativity: for a commutative hyperaddition with -1 = 1 satisfying reversibility, e ∈ (a ⊞ b) ⊞ c ⇔ (a ⊞ b) ∩ (c ⊞ e) ≠ ∅, so associativity is EQUIVALENT to: for all a, b, c, e ∈ H, (a ⊞ b) ∩ (c ⊞ e) ≠ ∅ ⇔ (b ⊞ c) ∩ (a ⊞ e) ≠ ∅ (i.e. "0 ∈ a ⊞ b ⊞ c ⊞ e" is a symmetric 4-ary relation). The structure is the same as a G-invariant S_3-symmetric set of "triangles" {a, b, c} (0 ∈ a ⊞ b ⊞ c) with the 4-point condition. (d) If moreover 1 ⊞ 1 = {0}, then H is a field: taking a = b in (c), (a ⊞ c) ∩ (a ⊞ e) ≠ ∅ ⇔ c = e, so for fixed a the |H| nonempty sets a ⊞ c (c ∈ H) are pairwise disjoint and cover H (d ∈ a ⊞ c for any c ∈ a ⊞ d), hence all singletons. So in a non-field with -1 = 1, D := (1 ⊞ 1) \ {0} is nonempty, and Q = {1} ∪ (1 ⊞ D) is never just {1}.
42	
43	Proof of (A5)(c), the step e ∈ (a⊞b)⊞c ⇔ (a⊞b)∩(c⊞e) ≠ ∅ when -1 = 1. If e ∈ t⊞c for some t ∈ a⊞b, then reversibility gives t ∈ e⊞(-c) = c⊞e. Conversely, if t ∈ (a⊞b)∩(c⊞e), then reversibility gives e ∈ t⊞c. Associativity says e ∈ (a⊞b)⊞c ⇔ e ∈ a⊞(b⊞c) = (b⊞c)⊞a, and by the first step this is the 4-point symmetry. For the converse direction, the 4-point symmetry for all a, b, c, e gives (a⊞b)⊞c = (b⊞c)⊞a as sets, and with commutativity this is associativity.
44	
45	## Part B. Proved results from earlier reports (verbatim excerpts)
46	
47	### B-1 (report round1_q1): composition rule; linear-derivation obstruction; quotients
48	## 1. The composition rule (proved)
49	
50	Here A and B are hypersums of finitely many terms, and t is an element.
51	
52	**Rule.** If 0 ∈ A⊞t and 0 ∈ B⊞(−t), then 0 ∈ A⊞B.
53	
54	*Proof.*
55	1. From 0 ∈ A⊞t there is an a ∈ A with 0 ∈ a⊞t. By uniqueness of negatives, a = −t, so −t ∈ A.
56	2. In the same way, from 0 ∈ B⊞(−t) we get t ∈ B.
57	3. Since 0 ∈ (−t)⊞t, it follows that 0 ∈ A⊞B. ∎
58	
59	There is also a weakening step: 0 ∈ C⊞a⊞(−a) holds for every element a and every sum C, so it carries no information.
60	
61	**What the rule does not give.** You cannot cancel a pair a, −a that sits inside a single relation: from 0 ∈ C⊞a⊞(−a) you cannot conclude 0 ∈ C. This is exactly where the field proof breaks down.
62	
63	## 2. Obstruction for "linear" proofs (proved)
64	
65	**Admissible derivations.** Call a derivation admissible if it uses only:
66	- the relations R_w : 0 ∈ wx⊞wy⊞(−w), for monomials w = ±xⁱyʲ (these come from distributivity applied to 0 ∈ x⊞y⊞(−1));
67	- the composition rule of §1.
68	
69	**Term count.** Composing k such relations needs k−1 cancellations. Each cancellation removes 2 terms, so the result has 3k − 2(k−1) = k+2 terms, counted with multiplicity.
70	
71	**Claim.** The target relation 0 ∈ x³⊞y³⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy⊞(−1) has 6 terms, so an admissible derivation would need exactly k = 4 relations. Taking x, y to be formal monomials, no choice of 4 relations works.
72	
73	*Proof.* Treat x, y as formal monomials, i.e. as independent indeterminates with no relations among their monomials.
74	1. **Which relations are forced.**
75	   - The term −1 can only come from R_1. Its terms are x, y, −1.
76	   - The term x³ can only come from R_{x²}. Its terms are x³, x²y, −x².
77	   - The term y³ can only come from R_{y²}. Its terms are xy², y³, −y².
78	2. **No cancellation among these three.** None of the nine terms of R_1, R_{x²}, R_{y²} is the negative of another of them, formally.
79	3. **The fourth relation is too small.** The single remaining relation would therefore have to supply all 3 cancellations, one for each of its 3 terms. That would remove 3 of the 6 unwanted terms x, y, x²y, −x², xy², −y².
80	4. **Conclusion.** At least 3 unwanted terms survive, and no xy term is produced at all. So no admissible derivation exists. ∎
81	
82	**Consequence.** The field identity has no "tree-shaped" realization.
83	- A natural field derivation uses x² = x − xy and x³ = x − xy − x²y, and then the step x²y + xy² = xy.
84	- That last step needs the *set* x²y⊞xy² to be contracted to its element xy.
85	- Hyperfield membership only allows replacing an element by a set that contains it, never contracting a set to one of its elements.
86	
87	Any affirmative proof must therefore use extra elements of H: auxiliary witnesses c taken from sums such as 1⊞1 or x⊞(−xy), together with relations satisfied by those witnesses. Arbitrary hyperfields need not have such relations. This, together with (B3), is evidence that the answer may be NO. It is only evidence, and it conflicts with the unrefereed computer search reported in (B5).
88	
89	## 3. Proved positive cases (taken from the task background, rechecked)
90	
91	- **z = 0.** Then 0 ∈ x⊞y forces y = −x, and the target set x³⊞(−x³) contains 0.
92	- **Quotient hyperfields F/U.** Choose representatives x', y', z' of the classes with x'+y'+z' = 0. Then x'³+y'³+z'³−3x'y'z' = 0 in F. Since x'³ ∈ [x]³ and x'y'z' ∈ [xyz], the class of 0 lies in the target sum.
93	
94	
95	### B-2 (report round1_q3): diagonal case and witness expansion
96	## Basic tool (proved)
97	If a ∈ S (a hypersum) then any multi-sum containing a as one summand is contained in the same multi-sum with S in place of a. This holds by associativity and because sums are unions over choices. It follows that replacing one summand c by a set that contains c can only shrink the target. That is the wrong direction for a proof, but it is used below in the following form: if c ∈ (p ⊞ q), then (… ⊞ p ⊞ q) ⊇ (… ⊞ c).
98	
99	## Proposition 1 (diagonal case, proved): if 1 ∈ x ⊞ x, then 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^3 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2.
100	Proof.
101	1. Multiplying 1 ∈ x ⊞ x by x^2 gives x^2 ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^3.
102	2. Therefore x^3 ⊞ x^3 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊇ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2, choosing x^2 from x^3 ⊞ x^3.
103	3. Multiplying by x gives x ∈ x^2 ⊞ x^2, so x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊞ x^2 ⊇ x ⊞ x.
104	4. Since 1 ∈ x ⊞ x, the target contains 1. ∎
105	
106	## Proposition 2 (expansion, proved): 1 ∈ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ w for some w ∈ xy(x ⊞ y).
107	Proof.
108	1. From 1 ∈ x ⊞ y we get x ∈ x^2 ⊞ xy and x^2 ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^2y, so x ∈ x^3 ⊞ x^2y ⊞ xy.
109	2. Similarly y ∈ y^3 ⊞ xy^2 ⊞ xy.
110	3. Hence 1 ∈ x ⊞ y ⊆ x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ (x^2y ⊞ xy^2), and x^2y ⊞ xy^2 = xy(x ⊞ y). ∎
111	
112	So the implication holds whenever this witness can be taken to be w = xy, i.e. whenever the element u ∈ x ⊞ y used here can be taken to be 1. In particular it holds whenever x ⊞ y = {1}. For example, this covers hyperfields in which x ⊞ y is a singleton for this pair.
113	
114	### B-3 (report round1_q4): absorption, class a⊞-a = H with -1 = 1, reduction to (C)
115	## Lemma 0 (absorption). For any a, H ⊞ a = H. Also, if S ∋ 0 then A ⊞ S ⊇ A for any set A.
116	Proof. Given c, pick h ∈ c⊞-a (this set is nonempty). By reversibility c ∈ h⊞a. The second claim holds because A⊞S ⊇ A⊞0 = A. ∎
117	
118	## (v) Hyperfields with a⊞-a = H for all a ≠ 0: the implication holds. (Proved.)
119	Normalize so that x, y ≠ 0. Case -1 = 1: then xy⊞xy = xy⊞-xy = H, so T ⊇ x³⊞y³⊞xy⊞H = H by Lemma 0, and 1 ∈ T. Case -1 ≠ 1: work in the unnormalized form. The target contains x³ ⊞ (-xyz ⊞ ...). If z = 0 the claim is trivial by (B2). Otherwise, if x³ = xyz then x³ ⊞ -xyz = H, so the target is H ⊞ (rest) = H, by Lemma 0. In general this argument needs one of x³, y³, z³ to equal xyz. So for (v) with -1 ≠ 1 only that special case is proved, and the rest is open. The hypothesis "a⊞-a ⊇ {0,a,-a}" gives nothing beyond this by the same method.
120	
121	## Reduction lemma for (i) and (ii). If 0 ∈ xy⊞xy⊞xy, or if 0 ∈ xy⊞xy, then the implication follows from the core claim
122	 (C) 1 ∈ x⊞y ⇒ 1 ∈ x³⊞y³⊞xy.
123	Proof. In the second case, T = (x³⊞y³⊞xy)⊞(xy⊞xy) ⊇ x³⊞y³⊞xy by Lemma 0. The first case is analogous, with core x³⊞y³ (stronger). ∎
124	- (i) If -1 = 1, then xy⊞xy ∋ 0, so the problem reduces to (C).
125	- (ii) If a⊞a = {a}, then xy⊞xy⊞xy = {xy}, so T = x³⊞y³⊞xy exactly, and the problem is equivalent to (C).
126	Restatement of (C): (x³⊞y³) ∩ (1⊞-xy) ≠ ∅. I could not prove (C) and found no counterexample to it. In a field of characteristic 2, x³+y³ = (x+y)(x²+xy+y²) = x²+xy+y² = 1+xy uses cancellation (x+y)² = x²+y², which is not available in a hyperfield (1 ∈ x⊞y gives only 1 ∈ x²⊞xy⊞xy⊞y²).
127	
128	
129	### B-4 (report round2_q3): check of the exponent-3 reduction (A4), and w, w^{-1} ∉ Q
130	## 1. Check of (B10) (proved)
131	Assume -1 = 1 and g^3 = 1 for every g in G. Put x^3 = y^3 = 1 and w = xy. Then T = 1 ⊞ 1 ⊞ w ⊞ w ⊞ w. By reversibility (with -1 = 1), 1 ∈ T if and only if 0 ∈ 1⊞1⊞1⊞w⊞w⊞w = Q ⊞ wQ. That holds if and only if Q ∩ (-wQ) = Q ∩ wQ ≠ ∅. Also y ∈ 1 ⊞ x if and only if 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, so w ranges over x ⊞ x^2. So (B10) is correct.
132	
133	## 2. New constraint (proved)
134	**Lemma.** If -1 = 1, then 1 ∈ Q = 1⊞1⊞1 always.
135	
136	*Proof.* 1 ∈ Q if and only if 0 ∈ 1⊞1⊞1⊞1 = (1⊞1) ⊞ (1⊞1). That holds if and only if (1⊞1) ∩ -(1⊞1) = (1⊞1) ∩ (1⊞1) is nonempty, which is true. ∎
137	
138	**Corollary.** In the exponent-3 class, a counterexample needs x and w ∈ x ⊞ x^2 with **w ∉ Q and w^{-1} = w^2 ∉ Q**.
139	- If w ∈ Q, then w = w·1 ∈ wQ (by the Lemma), so w ∈ Q ∩ wQ.
140	- If w^{-1} ∈ Q, then 1 = w·w^{-1} ∈ wQ and 1 ∈ Q.
141	
142	Together with (B10), a counterexample in this class also needs 1 ∉ 1 ⊞ 1 and w ≠ 1. In addition, Q must be disjoint from the whole translate wQ. Since 1 ∈ Q, this means wQ must avoid both 1 and w.
143	
144	
145	### B-5 (report round3_q1): triangle translation of the exponent-3 class; linear derivations fail there
146	## 1. Translation (proved, elementary)
147	
148	Write G = F_3^k additively. Group element g stands for the multiplicative element, and the hyperfield zero is written ∞. Let Δ be the set of unordered triples {a,b,c} of elements of G, with repetition allowed, such that 0_H ∈ a⊞b⊞c.
149	
150	**Statement.** By (B11c), the hyperfields of this class are exactly the families Δ that satisfy all of the following:
151	- Δ is invariant under translation by G;
152	- membership does not depend on the order of a, b, c;
153	- the 4-point condition holds.
154	
155	Here a⊞b = {c ∈ G : {a,b,c} ∈ Δ}, with ∞ added when a = b. Put S_g := 1⊞g ∩ G = {h : {0,g,h} ∈ Δ} and D = S_0.
156	
157	**Rules for the sets S_g.** Translation invariance and symmetry are equivalent to:
158	
159	h ∈ S_g ⇔ g ∈ S_h ⇔ −g ∈ S_{h−g} ⇔ −h ∈ S_{g−h}.
160	
161	These are the six images of {0,g,h} under the affine maps that permute the three points. They determine Δ completely.
162	
163	**Counterexample condition, by (B10)/(B11).** Define
164	- Q = {0} ∪ ⋃_{d∈D} S_d,
165	- w with {x, 2x, w} ∈ Δ for some x,
166	- and require Q ∩ (w+Q) = ∅.
167	
168	## 2. Linear derivations fail in the exponent-3 class (proved)
169	
170	**Admissible moves.** Only the following moves are allowed:
171	- the relations 0 ∈ mx ⊞ mx² ⊞ mw, for monomials m = x^i w^j;
172	- the pairs 0 ∈ a⊞a;
173	- disjoint union of zero-sums (if 0 ∈ A and 0 ∈ B then 0 ∈ A⊞B);
174	- composition (B5), which cancels one shared term between two different components.
175	
176	Cancelling a term inside a single component is not allowed (see B5).
177	
178	**Claim.** In the generic situation, where the 9 monomials x^i w^j are distinct, no such derivation produces 0 ∈ 1⊞1⊞1⊞w⊞w⊞w. (Specific Δ might create extra coincidences among the monomials; that case is not covered.)
179	
180	**Proof.**
181	
182	*Step 1 (counting).* A component built from n triangles linked in a tree has n+2 remaining terms. A pair component has 2 terms. Attaching a pair to an existing term changes nothing, because 0∈A⊞a together with 0∈a⊞a gives back 0∈A⊞a. To get 6 terms, the possible shapes are:
183	- (i) a single tree of 4 triangles;
184	- (ii) a tree of 2 triangles plus one pair;
185	- (iii) two separate triangles.
186	
187	*Step 2 (shapes (ii) and (iii)).* Each triangle has 3 distinct terms. Shape (ii) would need three equal leftover terms from two triangles; shape (iii) would need a triangle {1,1,w} or {1,w,w}. Both are impossible.
188	
189	*Step 3 (shape (i), reduction to the group ring).* Reduce mod 2 in R = F_2[x,w]/(x³−1, w³−1) ≅ (F_2 × F_4)⊗(F_2 × F_4). Let f be the sum of the four chosen m's. Then f·(x+x²+w) = 1+w + 2(cancelled pairs) ≡ 1+w.
190	
191	*Step 4 (solving at x = 1).* At x = 1 we have x+x² = 0. The equation becomes f(1,w)·w = 1+w, so f(1,w) = 1+w².
192	
193	*Step 5 (solving at x = ω).* At x = ω we have x+x² = 1. The equation becomes f(ω,w)(1+w) = 1+w, so f(ω,w) ≡ 1 mod (1+w+w²).
194	
195	*Step 6 (all solutions).* Write f = a + b w + c w². The conditions give a = 1, b = 0, c = 1+x+x², up to the kernel, which is h(x)(1+w+w²) with h ∈ {0, x+x², 1+x, 1+x²}. So the solutions are
196	
197	f = 1 + (1+x+x²)w² + h(x)(1+w+w²).
198	
199	The 4-term solutions include:
200	- {1, w², xw², x²w²};
201	- x + (1+x)w + x²w², i.e. {x, w, xw, x²w²}.
202	
203	*Step 7 (checking multiplicities).* Expand the integer multiset of terms for either 4-term solution. It contains 1 and w exactly once each, and five other monomials exactly twice each. For example, the first solution gives x, x², xw², x²w², w² twice each. The target 1,1,1,w,w,w needs coefficient 3 on both 1 and w. Moreover, 3 tree edges can cancel only 3 of the 5 doubled pairs. So shape (i) fails as well. ∎
204	
205	**Interpretation.** Unlike the generic case (B6), the mod-2 equation is solvable here. The obstruction comes from the integer multiplicities and the tree structure, not from parity. An affirmative proof would need witnesses from D = (1⊞1)\{0} or other auxiliary elements.
206	
207	
208	### B-6 (report round3_q2): with -1 = 1, exchanges are compositions; no linear derivation proves (C)
209	## 1. Exchanges are compositions
210	
211	Assume -1 = 1. By (B11)(c), "0 ∈ a⊞b⊞c⊞e" holds iff (a⊞b)∩(c⊞e) ≠ ∅, and this relation is symmetric in a, b, c, e.
212	
213	A 4-point exchange only re-reads this symmetric relation. The only way to *produce* a new 4-term (or longer) relation from triangles is to glue two relations along a shared element t. This is the composition rule (B5): from 0∈A⊞t and 0∈B⊞t, conclude 0∈A⊞B (here -t = t).
214	
215	So a chain built only from the hypothesis triangles {g, gx, gy} (all g ∈ G, coming from y ∈ 1⊞x), using exchanges, is a "linear derivation" in the sense of (B6).
216	
217	## 2. Proposition: no linear derivation proves (C) when -1 = 1
218	
219	**Claim.** No linear derivation proves (C).
220	
221	**Proof.**
222	1. Suppose a derivation glues k relations R_w = {w, wx, wy} (monomial labels w; repeats allowed) into a tree with k-1 gluings.
223	2. Each gluing removes 2 terms. The relations contribute 3k terms, so the final sum has 3k - 2(k-1) = k + 2 terms.
224	3. The target 0 ∈ 1⊞x^3⊞y^3⊞xy has 4 terms, so k = 2.
225	4. Two relations R_w and R_{w'} share a term only if w' ∈ {wx, wy, wx^{-1}, wy^{-1}, wxy^{-1}, wyx^{-1}}. Gluing them leaves 4 terms of the form w·{…}.
226	5. For the result to equal {1, x^3, y^3, xy} as monomials, the exponents would have to match. Checking all 6 cases, none does: the glued 4-sets have total degree spread at most 2, but {1, x^3} has spread 3.
227	
228	So the derivation is impossible. ∎
229	
230	**Why the field proof does not transfer.** Over F_2 one has 1+x^3+y^3+xy = (1+x+y)(1+x+y+x^2+xy+y^2). This combines the six relations R_1, R_x, R_y, R_{x^2}, R_{xy}, R_{y^2}, which have 18 terms. Reaching 4 terms needs 7 cancelled pairs, but a tree on 6 relations allows only 5 gluings. Closing the extra cycles would need the inference "0∈C⊞a⊞a ⇒ 0∈C", which is invalid in hyperfields.
231	
232	The same argument covers the weaker target 1∈T, with T = x^3⊞y^3⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy. That target has 6 terms, so k = 4. The 12 terms of four relations, glued in a tree, would have to give exactly {1, x^3, y^3, xy, xy, xy}. The coefficient polynomial would have to be a degree-2 multiple of (1+x+y) matching the field identity, which needs 6 relations, not 4. So this is impossible too, as in (B6).
233	
234	**Consequence.** Any affirmative proof must use auxiliary existential elements, such as d ∈ (1⊞1)\{0} or witnesses u ∈ x⊞y with u ≠ 1, together with the axioms they satisfy. Exchange chains alone, which are idea (a) of the task, cannot work.
235	
236	
237	### B-7 (report round3_q4): class a⊞-a = H with -1 ≠ 1, coincidences; union-type hyperfields satisfy the claim
238	## 1. Coincidences in the class a ⊞ -a = H (proved)
239	
240	Let H be a hyperfield with a ⊞ -a = H for every a ≠ 0.
241	
242	**Lemma 1.** Let S be a multi-sum whose summands include two nonzero opposite elements a and -a. Then S = H.
243	
244	*Proof.* Write S = (a ⊞ -a) ⊞ R = H ⊞ R. We have H ⊞ r = H for every element r: given h, pick h' ∈ h ⊞ -r; by reversibility h ∈ h' ⊞ r. Applying this to each summand of R gives S = H. ∎
245	
246	**Corollary.** If two of the summands of T ⊞ (-1) are opposite, namely the summands x^3, y^3, xy, xy, xy, -1, then T ⊞ (-1) = H ∋ 0 and the claim holds. So the claim holds whenever one of the following holds:
247	- x^3 = -y^3,
248	- x^3 = 1 or y^3 = 1 (opposite to -1),
249	- xy = 1,
250	- xy = -x^3, i.e. y = -x^2,
251	- xy = -y^3, i.e. x = -y^2,
252	- xy = -xy, which is impossible because -1 ≠ 1.
253	
254	Only the "generic" case remains, where none of these coincidences occurs. In that case xy ⊞ xy does not contain 0, because 0 ∈ a ⊞ a forces a = -a. So nothing more can be extracted from Lemma 1. I could not settle this generic case.
255	
256	## 2. A natural family in this class satisfies the claim (proved)
257	
258	**Construction.** Let G be any abelian group containing an element -1 of order 2. Put H = G ∪ {0}, with 0 neutral, and for nonzero a, b define:
259	- a ⊞ b = {a, b} if b ≠ -a (in particular a ⊞ a = {a});
260	- a ⊞ -a = H.
261	
262	**Claim.** H is a hyperfield.
263	
264	*Proof.* Every multi-sum is computed as follows. If the nonzero summands contain an opposite pair, the sum is H. Otherwise it is the set of the distinct nonzero summands, or {0} if every summand is 0. This rule gives the same set under every bracketing, so ⊞ is associative. It is also commutative.
265	
266	Reversibility: suppose c ∈ a ⊞ b with a, b ≠ 0.
267	- If b = -a, then c is arbitrary, and a ∈ c ⊞ a in each subcase c = 0, c = a, c = -a, or c generic, where c ⊞ a = {c, a}.
268	- If b = a, then c = a, and a ∈ a ⊞ -a = H.
269	- Otherwise c ∈ {a, b}. If c = a, then a ∈ a ⊞ -b = {a, -b}. If c = b, then a ∈ b ⊞ -b = H.
270	
271	The cases where a or b is 0 are trivial. Distributivity holds because multiplication by w maps opposite pairs to opposite pairs. ∎
272	
273	The sign hyperfield is the case G = {±1}.
274	
275	**Claim.** The implication holds in this H.
276	
277	*Proof.* Suppose 1 ∈ x ⊞ y with x, y ≠ 0. Then either y = -x or 1 ∈ {x, y}.
278	- If y = -x, then x^3 and y^3 are opposite, so T = H.
279	- If x = 1 or y = 1, then 1 is a summand of T. So T is either H or the set of its summands, and either way 1 ∈ T. ∎
280	
281	So "union-type" hyperfields in this class satisfy the claim. A counterexample must have sums that are genuinely larger than the set of summands but smaller than H.
282	
283	
284	## Part C. Computational evidence (unrefereed) and coordinator observations
285	
286	(C1) Exhaustive computer search over all hyperfields H = G ∪ {0} with |G| ≤ 9 (every abelian group of order ≤ 8, plus Z9 and Z3×Z3) found no counterexample. Any counterexample has at least 11 elements.
287	
288	(C2) Exponent-3, characteristic-2 triangle systems (the class of (A4)/(A5), in the additive notation of B-5). The coordinator ran exhaustive constraint searches for counterexamples, i.e. structures with a triangle {x, x^2, w} and Q ∩ wQ = ∅. None was found:
289	- on F_3^3, among systems invariant under translations and under v ↦ −v;
290	- on F_3^3, among systems invariant under multiplication by the order-13 subgroup of F_27^*;
291	- on F_3^4, among systems invariant under multiplication by F_81^*.
292	
293	In every non-field associative system the coordinator enumerated with 1 ∉ 1⊞1 (F_3^2 and F_3^3 with various multiplicative symmetries), Q = 1⊞1⊞1 contained all of G, so the claim held trivially. A counterexample in this class needs Q ∩ wQ = ∅, hence |Q| ≤ |G|/2. That requires a "sparse" structure, which small groups do not admit. Any counterexample in this class must live on a larger group F_3^k (k ≥ 5, or infinite rank) and have small sums.
294	
295	(C3) Krasner extensions (-1 = 1 and a⊞a = {0, a}) correspond to projective geometries with point set G, on which G acts regularly by multiplication; here a⊞b is the line through a and b with a and b removed, for a ≠ b. In this class the claim becomes an incidence statement. All known such geometries are Desarguesian, hence quotients, hence satisfy the claim. So this class was judged unpromising, but it has not been refuted as a source of counterexamples.
296	
297	(C4) Free-hyperfield reformulation (coordinator's observation, not refereed). Build a hyperfield "freely" from generators x, y and the single relation 1 ∈ x⊞y, by a chase: repeatedly add every membership forced by distributivity, commutativity and reversibility, and for every associativity instance and every empty sum add a fresh group generator as witness. If the resulting limit is a hyperfield (a statement still to be checked), then it maps to every hyperfield containing such x, y by a membership-preserving map. The question is then equivalent to whether 1 ∈ T holds in this free object. A counterexample amounts to an invariant of the chase steps that the target violates.
298

27	## Part A. Conventions and coordinator facts
28	
29	(A1) Conventions. A hyperfield is H = G ∪ {0}, G an abelian multiplicative group, with a commutative, associative multivalued addition ⊞ (sums of several terms are unions over all choices, well defined by associativity), 0 neutral, each a has a unique -a with 0 ∈ a ⊞ -a, reversibility (c ∈ a ⊞ b ⇒ a ∈ c ⊞ -b), and distributivity w(a ⊞ b) = wa ⊞ wb for single elements w. -a = (-1)a with (-1)^2 = 1; possibly -1 = 1. Useful: 0 ∈ A ⊞ B iff A ∩ (-B) ≠ ∅; if c ∈ p ⊞ q then (S ⊞ p ⊞ q) ⊇ (S ⊞ c) ("merging two summands into an element of their sum only shrinks the sum"); H ⊞ a = H for every a; if 0 ∈ S then A ⊞ S ⊇ A.

31	(A2) Normalization. z = 0 is trivial (y = -x, and 0 ∈ x^3 ⊞ -x^3). For z ≠ 0, scaling by -1/z makes the question equivalent to: for nonzero x, y with 1 ∈ x ⊞ y, is 1 ∈ T := x^3 ⊞ y^3 ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ⊞ xy ?

165	
166	**Admissible moves.** Only the following moves are allowed:
167	- the relations 0 ∈ mx ⊞ mx² ⊞ mw, for monomials m = x^i w^j;
168	- the pairs 0 ∈ a⊞a;
169	- disjoint union of zero-sums (if 0 ∈ A and 0 ∈ B then 0 ∈ A⊞B);

176	**Proof.**

178	*Step 1 (counting).* A component built from n triangles linked in a tree has n+2 remaining terms. A pair component has 2 terms. Attaching a pair to an existing term changes nothing, because 0∈A⊞a together with 0∈a⊞a gives back 0∈A⊞a. To get 6 terms, the possible shapes are:
179	- (i) a single tree of 4 triangles;
180	- (ii) a tree of 2 triangles plus one pair;
181	- (iii) two separate triangles.

183	*Step 2 (shapes (ii) and (iii)).* Each triangle has 3 distinct terms. Shape (ii) would need three equal leftover terms from two triangles; shape (iii) would need a triangle {1,1,w} or {1,w,w}. Both are impossible.

**Verdict: COUNTEREXAMPLE to (N). The answer to the problem is NO.**

The counterexample is a hyperfield extension of the Krasner hyperfield ("projective-geometry type", -1 = 1, a⊞a = {0,a}). Its point set is the infinite cyclic group Z, and its lines are the translates of a *perfect difference set* D ⊂ Z. D is built greedily so that it contains a prescribed configuration that a Desarguesian plane would not allow. Every axiom is checked below, and associativity is proved for all triples.

## 1. Hyperfields from projective planes with a regular abelian group

**Setup.** Let G be an abelian group (written multiplicatively). Let P be a projective-plane-like incidence structure with point set G, satisfying:
- (P1) any two distinct points lie on exactly one line;
- (P2) any two distinct lines meet;
- (P3) every line has at least 5 points;
- (P4) the set of lines is invariant under multiplication by every w ∈ G.

From (P1), two distinct lines meet in exactly one point. Write L(a,b) for the line through the distinct points a and b.

Define H = G ∪ {0}. Let 0 be neutral (0⊞a = {a}), and for nonzero a, b set
- a ⊞ a = {0, a};
- a ⊞ b = L(a,b) \ {a, b} for a ≠ b.

Multiplication is the group law, extended by 0·h = 0.

**Proposition 1.** H is a hyperfield with -a = a for every a.

*Proof.*

*Commutativity and nonemptiness.* Both are clear: L(a,b) has at least 5 points, so a ⊞ b is nonempty.

*Negatives.* For a ≠ b, both nonzero, a⊞b ⊆ G, so 0 ∉ a⊞b. Also 0 ∈ a⊞a. Hence the unique negative of a is a itself, and -1 = 1.

*Reversibility.* We need: c ∈ a⊞b ⇒ a ∈ c⊞(-b) = c⊞b.
- a = 0: then c = b, and 0 ∈ b⊞b.
- b = 0: then c = a, and a ∈ a⊞0.
- a = b ≠ 0: then c ∈ {0, a}. If c = 0, then a ∈ 0⊞a. If c = a, then a ∈ a⊞a.
- a ≠ b, both nonzero: then c ∈ L(a,b) \ {a,b}. So c ≠ b and L(c,b) = L(a,b), giving c⊞b = L(a,b) \ {c,b}. This set contains a, because a ≠ c and a ≠ b.

*Distributivity.* Multiplication by w ∈ G permutes points and maps lines to lines (P4). Hence w·L(a,b) = L(wa,wb), so w(a⊞b) = wa⊞wb. For w = 0 the identity is trivial.

*Associativity.* If one of a, b, c is 0, both (a⊞b)⊞c and a⊞(b⊞c) equal the sum of the other two, because 0 is neutral. For a, b, c nonzero we show that S(a,b,c) := (a⊞b)⊞c depends only on the multiset {a,b,c}. Then (a⊞b)⊞c = (b⊞c)⊞a = a⊞(b⊞c).

1. **a = b = c.** S = (0⊞a) ∪ (a⊞a) = {0, a}.

2. **Multiset {a, a, c} with a ≠ c; put L = L(a,c).** The two bracketings give the same set.
   - (a⊞a)⊞c = (0⊞c) ∪ (a⊞c) = {c} ∪ (L \ {a,c}) = L \ {a}.
   - (a⊞c)⊞a = ⋃_{p ∈ L\{a,c}} (p⊞a) = ⋃_{p ∈ L\{a,c}} (L \ {p,a}). This union is L \ {a}, because L \ {a,c} has at least two elements (P3).

3. **a, b, c distinct and collinear on L.** Here a⊞b = L \ {a,b}, which contains c. Then
   S = (c⊞c) ∪ ⋃_{p ∈ L\{a,b,c}} (L \ {p,c}) = {0, c} ∪ (L \ {c}) = L ∪ {0}.
   The middle step uses that L \ {a,b,c} has at least two elements (P3). The result is symmetric in a, b, c.

4. **a, b, c not collinear.** We claim S = G \ (L(a,b) ∪ L(b,c) ∪ L(a,c)), which is symmetric in a, b, c. By definition, S = ⋃_{p ∈ L(a,b)\{a,b}} (L(p,c) \ {p,c}). Note p ≠ c always, since c ∉ L(a,b).
   - 0 ∉ S.
   - c ∉ S.
   - If q ∈ L(a,b) \ {a,b}: L(p,c) ≠ L(a,b), so L(p,c) ∩ L(a,b) = {p}. Membership q ∈ L(p,c) would force q = p, which is excluded.
   - If q ∈ L(a,c) \ {a,c} and q ∈ L(p,c) \ {p,c}: then L(p,c) = L(q,c) = L(a,c), so p ∈ L(a,c) ∩ L(a,b) = {a}, which is excluded. The case q ∈ L(b,c) is the same, and a, b ∉ S follows the same way.
   - Any other point q (on none of the three lines): put p := L(q,c) ∩ L(a,b) (P2). Then p ≠ a, since otherwise q ∈ L(a,c); likewise p ≠ b; and p ≠ q, since q ∉ L(a,b). Hence q ∈ L(p,c) \ {p,c} with p ∈ L(a,b) \ {a,b}, so q ∈ S.

This covers all multisets of three nonzero elements, so ⊞ is associative. ∎

(This is the known correspondence between hyperfield extensions of the Krasner hyperfield and projective geometries with a regular abelian group, due to Connes–Consani, cited from memory. The proof above is self-contained, so the citation is not needed.)

## 2. What the target is in such an H

**Lemma 2.** Let x, y ∈ G be such that:
- 1, x, y are distinct and collinear;
- x^3, y^3, xy are distinct and lie on a line M with 1 ∉ M.

Then 1 ∈ x⊞y, but 1 ∉ T := x^3⊞y^3⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy.

*Proof.*
- 1 ∈ L(x,y) \ {x,y} = x⊞y.
- xy⊞xy⊞xy = (0⊞xy) ∪ (xy⊞xy) = {0, xy}.
- Hence T = (x^3⊞y^3) ∪ (x^3⊞y^3⊞xy).
  - The first part is x^3⊞y^3 = M \ {x^3, y^3}.
  - The second part is M ∪ {0}, by case 3 of the associativity proof.
- So T = M ∪ {0}, which does not contain 1. ∎

**The original question.** Take z = 1 (= -1). Then 0 ∈ x⊞y⊞z, since 1 ∈ x⊞y and 0 ∈ 1⊞1. Since -xyz = xy, the target sum is x^3⊞y^3⊞1⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy = T⊞1. By uniqueness of negatives, 0 ∈ T⊞1 iff 1 = -1 ∈ T, which is false. So the implication fails.

## 3. A plane with the required configuration: perfect difference sets in Z

Now write G = Z additively. Point n corresponds to the group element t^n, so 1 ↔ 0 and multiplication ↔ addition.

Call D ⊂ Z a *perfect difference set* if every nonzero integer has exactly one representation d - d' with d, d' ∈ D.

**Lemma 3.** If D is an infinite perfect difference set, the lines {g + D : g ∈ Z} satisfy (P1)–(P4).

*Proof.*
- (P1): points p ≠ q lie on g + D iff p - g = d1 and q - g = d2 with d1, d2 ∈ D. Then p - q = d1 - d2, and this representation exists and is unique. So g = p - d1 exists and is unique.
- (P2): lines g + D and h + D with g ≠ h share the point g + d1 = h + d2, where (d1, d2) is the representation of h - g = d1 - d2. (Every nonzero integer has one.)
- (P3): every line is infinite.
- (P4): the set of lines is translation invariant by construction. ∎

**Lemma 4.** There is a perfect difference set D ⊂ Z with D ⊇ D_0 := {0, 1, 4, 103, 105, 112} and 100 ∉ D.

*Proof.*

*D_0 is Sidon.* Its 15 positive differences are 1, 4, 3 (within {0,1,4}), then 2, 9, 7 (within {103,105,112}), then 103, 105, 112, 102, 104, 111, 99, 101, 108. These are pairwise distinct, so every nonzero integer has at most one representation as a difference of elements of D_0.

*Inductive step.* Suppose a finite Sidon set D_k is given. Let:
- m be the least positive integer that is not a difference of D_k;
- R = max |d| over d ∈ D_k;
- N be an integer with N > 3R + m.

Put D_{k+1} = D_k ∪ {N, N+m}. The new positive differences are m, the numbers N - d, and the numbers N + m - d (d ∈ D_k). We check they are distinct from each other and from the old ones:
- All N - d and N + m - d are larger than 2R, which bounds the old differences, and larger than m.
- Values N - d are pairwise distinct, and so are values N + m - d.
- N - d = N + m - d' would give d' - d = m, contradicting the choice of m.
- m is not an old difference, by choice.

So D_{k+1} is Sidon and m is now a difference. Also N, N+m > 336 > 100, so 100 is never added.

*Covering.* The least uncovered positive integer strictly increases from step to step, so every positive integer is eventually a difference. By symmetry every negative integer is too.

*Conclusion.* D = ⋃ D_k is infinite. It is Sidon, since any two representations already lie in a common finite D_k, so every nonzero integer is represented at most once. Every nonzero integer is represented at least once by the covering step. Finally 100 ∉ D. ∎

## 4. The counterexample

Let H be the hyperfield of Proposition 1, built on G = Z with lines g + D, where D is the set from Lemma 4. Take x ↔ 1 and y ↔ 4 (additive notation), and z = 1_H ↔ 0. We check the hypotheses of Lemma 2.
- **The points 1_H, x, y** are 0, 1, 4. They are distinct and lie on the line D.
- **The points x^3, y^3, xy** are 3, 12, 5. They are distinct and lie on the line M = -100 + D, since 103, 112, 105 ∈ D.
- **1_H is not on M.** The point 0 lies on M iff 100 ∈ D, which is false.

So by Lemma 2, 1 ∈ x⊞y but 1 ∉ x^3⊞y^3⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy = M ∪ {0}. Equivalently, 0 ∈ x⊞y⊞z but 0 ∉ x^3⊞y^3⊞z^3⊞-xyz⊞-xyz⊞-xyz.

**Remarks.**
- H is necessarily a non-quotient hyperfield. A Desarguesian plane, i.e. a quotient F/K^*, would force 1 ∈ M by the field identity.
- H is infinite. This agrees with the background search, which found no counterexample with |G| ≤ 9.
- The derivation of (N) from the problem given in the task is correct. Here the counterexample is checked directly in the original form, with z = 1 = -1.

**Status.** Everything above is proved; no part of the argument is left open. One question is not settled here: whether a *finite* counterexample exists. It would need, for instance, a finite non-Desarguesian plane with a regular abelian group, whose existence is a well-known open problem (cited from memory), or a different construction.

# round4_q1 — answer

**Verdict: COUNTEREXAMPLE to (N).** So the answer to the Question is **NO**.

The counterexample is an infinite hyperfield extension of the Krasner hyperfield (-1 = 1, a⊞a = {0,a}). It is built from a non-Desarguesian cyclic projective plane over the infinite cyclic group, made by M. Hall's greedy "free extension" of planar difference sets. (Hall, *Cyclic projective planes*, Duke Math. J. 1947, cited from memory. Everything Hall-related is proved below from scratch, so the citation is not needed.) Concretely, x = t, y = t^10, z = 1 = -1.

## 1. Planar difference sets in Z (proved)

A finite set S ⊂ Z is **Sidon** if the map (s,s') ↦ s - s' is injective on pairs with s ≠ s'. Equivalently, all positive differences s - s' (s > s') are pairwise distinct: a coincidence between two negative differences becomes one between positive differences after swapping each pair. A set D ⊂ Z is a **planar difference set** if every nonzero integer n has exactly one representation n = d - d' with d, d' ∈ D.

**Lemma 1 (Hall's extension).** Let S_0 be a finite Sidon set with M_0 = max_{s∈S_0}|s|. Then there is a planar difference set D ⊇ S_0 with D \ S_0 ⊂ (3M_0, ∞).

*Proof.* Build finite Sidon sets S_0 ⊂ S_1 ⊂ … inductively. Given S_k, let M_k = max|s| over s ∈ S_k. Let n_k be the least positive integer that is not a difference of S_k (it exists because S_k is finite). Choose an integer c_k > 3M_k + n_k and put S_{k+1} = S_k ∪ {c_k, c_k + n_k}. Note c_k > M_k, so both elements are new.

The positive differences of S_{k+1} are of three kinds:
- the old ones, all ≤ 2M_k;
- n_k;
- c_k - s and c_k + n_k - s for s ∈ S_k.

Each number of the third kind is ≥ c_k - M_k > 2M_k + n_k, so it differs from every old difference and from n_k. Two numbers c_k - s, c_k - s' (or c_k + n_k - s, c_k + n_k - s') agree only if s = s'. And c_k - s = c_k + n_k - s' would give s' - s = n_k, a difference of S_k, which contradicts the choice of n_k. Finally, n_k is not an old difference. So S_{k+1} is Sidon.

Every positive integer ≤ n_k is a difference of S_{k+1}: those below n_k already were differences of S_k, and n_k = (c_k + n_k) - c_k. Hence n_{k+1} > n_k, so n_k → ∞.

Put D = ⋃ S_k. Every positive n is ≤ some n_k, so it is a difference of D. Any two representations of n lie in a common S_k, which is Sidon, so they coincide. Negative n follow by swapping. Every added element exceeds 3M_k ≥ 3M_0. ∎

**The specific set.** Take S_0 = {0, 1, 10, 1003, 1011, 1030}. Its 15 positive differences are

1, 9, 10 (from {0,1,10}); 8, 19, 27 (from {1003,1011,1030}); 1003, 1011, 1030, 1002, 1010, 1029, 993, 1001, 1020 (cross differences).

These are pairwise distinct, so S_0 is Sidon. Let D be given by Lemma 1. Then D ∩ (-∞, 3090] = S_0. In particular **1000 ∉ D**, and D is infinite, because a finite set has only finitely many differences.

## 2. The hyperfield H_D (all axioms verified)

Let G = {t^n : n ∈ Z} be the infinite cyclic group and H = G ∪ {0}, with the usual multiplication (0·a = 0). The **lines** are L_g = {t^{g+d} : d ∈ D} for g ∈ Z. Each line is infinite.

**Lemma 2 (projective plane).**
- (a) Two distinct points t^m, t^n lie on exactly one common line, called ℓ(t^m, t^n).
- (b) Two distinct lines meet in exactly one point.
- (c) Multiplication by t^k maps L_g to L_{g+k}, so it maps lines to lines.

*Proof.*
- (a) t^m, t^n ∈ L_g iff m - g = d and n - g = d' with d, d' ∈ D. Then m - n = d - d', which has a unique representation, and g = m - d. Conversely, that representation gives such a g.
- (b) t^m ∈ L_g ∩ L_h iff m - g = d and m - h = d' with d, d' ∈ D. Then h - g = d - d' ≠ 0, which has a unique representation, and m = g + d.
- (c) This is clear. ∎

**Definition of ⊞.** For a, b ∈ G:
- 0 ⊞ a = a ⊞ 0 = {a}, and 0 ⊞ 0 = {0};
- a ⊞ a = {0, a};
- a ⊞ b = ℓ(a,b) \ {a, b} for a ≠ b.

So a "point on a line" and "collinear" refer to Lemma 2.

**Axioms.**
1. **Commutativity.** This is clear from the definition.
2. **Nonempty sums.** All lines are infinite, so a ⊞ b ≠ ∅ for a ≠ b.
3. **Negatives.** For a, b ∈ G we have 0 ∈ a ⊞ b iff a = b. Also 0 ∈ 0 ⊞ b iff b = 0. So -a = a is the unique negative, and -1 = 1.
4. **Distributivity.** For w = t^k this follows from Lemma 2(c), since multiplication by w preserves ℓ, equality and 0. For w = 0 both sides are {0}.
5. **Reversibility.** Since -b = b, we must show c ∈ a ⊞ b ⇒ a ∈ c ⊞ b.
   - a = 0: then c = b, and 0 ∈ b ⊞ b.
   - b = 0: then c = a, and a ∈ a ⊞ 0.
   - a = b ≠ 0: then c ∈ {0, a}, and a ∈ 0 ⊞ a and a ∈ a ⊞ a.
   - a ≠ b, both nonzero: then c ∈ ℓ(a,b) \ {a,b}. So c ≠ b and ℓ(c,b) = ℓ(a,b) ∋ a with a ∉ {c,b}, hence a ∈ c ⊞ b.
6. **Associativity.**
   - **Symmetry of membership.** For a, b, c ∈ H put Ψ(a,b,c) :⇔ a ∈ b ⊞ c. By reversibility (with -1 = 1) and commutativity, Ψ is invariant under all permutations of its arguments.
   - **Step (i).** e ∈ t ⊞ c ⇔ t ∈ e ⊞ c, which is the symmetry of Ψ. Since (a⊞b)⊞c = ⋃_{s∈a⊞b} s⊞c, we get e ∈ (a⊞b)⊞c ⇔ R(a,b,c,e), where R(a,b,c,e) :⇔ (a⊞b) ∩ (c⊞e) ≠ ∅.
   - **Reduction.** Likewise e ∈ a⊞(b⊞c) = (b⊞c)⊞a ⇔ R(b,c,a,e). So associativity follows once R is invariant under all permutations of its four arguments. R is invariant under swapping inside each pair and under swapping the two pairs, so it suffices to show R(a,b,c,e) ⇔ R(a,c,b,e).
   - **Some argument is 0.**
     - R(0,b,c,e) = Ψ(b,c,e) and R(0,c,b,e) = Ψ(c,b,e).
     - R(a,b,c,0) = Ψ(c,a,b) and R(a,c,b,0) = Ψ(b,a,c).
     - R(a,0,c,e) = Ψ(a,c,e) and R(a,c,0,e) = Ψ(e,a,c). The case c = 0 is symmetric to this one.

     All of these agree by the symmetry of Ψ.
   - **All arguments nonzero.** Directly from the definition:
     - for a = b and c = e, R is true (0 lies in both sums);
     - for a = b and c ≠ e, R ⇔ a ∈ ℓ(c,e) \ {c,e};
     - for a ≠ b and c ≠ e, R is true if ℓ(a,b) = ℓ(c,e) (an infinite line minus at most 4 points is nonempty); otherwise the two lines meet in one point p, and R ⇔ p ∉ {a,b,c,e}.

     We sort by the multiplicity pattern of the multiset {a,b,c,e}:
     - **{a,a,a,a}.** R is always true.
     - **{a,a,a,c}, c ≠ a.** Every arrangement pairs {a,a} with {a,c}, and a ∉ ℓ(a,c) \ {a,c}. So R is always false.
     - **{a,a,c,c}, c ≠ a.** The pairing {a,a}|{c,c} is true. The pairing {a,c}|{a,c} uses the same line, so it is also true. So R is always true.
     - **{a,a,c,e}, with a, c, e distinct.** In the pairing {a,a}|{c,e}, R ⇔ a,c,e are collinear. In the pairing {a,c}|{a,e}, either the lines are equal (a,c,e collinear: true) or they meet exactly at a (false). So R ⇔ a,c,e are collinear in every arrangement.
     - **Four distinct points, pairing {a,b}|{c,e}.** Claim: R ⇔ (all four collinear) or (no three collinear).

       If ℓ(a,b) = ℓ(c,e), all four are collinear and R is true.

       Otherwise let p be the meeting point. Every triple of the four points contains a pair from one side and one point from the other side. If such a triple is collinear, that one point lies on both lines, so it equals p. Conversely, if p is one of the four points, say p = a, then a,c,e are collinear. Also b ∉ ℓ(c,e), because otherwise b = p = a. So in this case "R false" means exactly that some three are collinear but not all four.

     So in all patterns R depends only on the multiset {a,b,c,e}. Hence R is fully symmetric, and ⊞ is associative. ∎

So H_D is a hyperfield. (It is a Krasner extension in the sense of Connes–Consani, which I recall without relying on it.)

## 3. The counterexample

Take x = t, y = t^10, z = 1 = t^0. Then:
- xyz = t^11 and -xyz = t^11;

# Answer to round4_q7: NO, the statement (N) is false (task part (b))

**Result (proved below).** There is a hyperfield H with -1 = 1, and elements x, y, z with 0 ∈ x⊞y⊞z, such that
0 ∉ x^3⊞y^3⊞z^3⊞-xyz⊞-xyz⊞-xyz.
So the answer to the Question is **No**. In the normalized form (N), this hyperfield has x, y ∈ G with 1 ∈ x⊞y and 1 ∉ x^3⊞y^3⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy.

The counterexample does not use a term model of the zero-sum calculus. It is an extension of the Krasner hyperfield built from a projective plane. The plane is a *free* (non-Desarguesian) projective plane whose point set is a free abelian group of countable rank, with that group acting regularly by translations. In such a plane the configuration "1, x, y collinear; 1, x^3, xy collinear; y^3 not on that line" can be imposed. Desarguesian planes, which are quotients, forbid it. The coordinator's remark (C3) judged this class unpromising, but that remark only considered Desarguesian geometries.

Notation: the multiplicative group G is written additively as A. The group identity "1" is the element 0 of A. The zero of the hyperfield is written ∞.

## 1. Projective planes with a regular abelian group give hyperfields

**Lemma 1.** Let A be an abelian group (written additively), and let 𝓛 be a family of subsets of A ("lines") such that:
- (P1) any two distinct points lie on exactly one line;
- (P2) any two distinct lines meet in exactly one point;
- (P3) every line has at least 4 points;
- (P4) 𝓛 is invariant under all translations p ↦ p + w.

Put H = A ∪ {∞}. Multiplication is the group law of A, with ∞·h = ∞. Every element is its own negative. Addition is defined as follows:
- ∞ ⊞ a = a ⊞ ∞ = {a};
- a ⊞ a = {∞, a} for a ∈ A;
- for distinct a, b ∈ A, a ⊞ b = ℓ(a,b) \ {a,b}, where ℓ(a,b) is the line through a and b.

Then H is a hyperfield in the sense of the task. Here -1 = 1, i.e. -a = a.

*Proof.* All sums are nonempty, since lines have at least 3 points. Commutativity is clear. Multiplication by w ∈ A is the translation by w. That map sends lines to lines (P4), fixes ∞, and sends {∞, a} to {∞, a+w}, so w(a⊞b) = wa⊞wb.

*The ternary relation.* Define T(p,q,r) :⇔ r ∈ p⊞q, for p, q, r ∈ H. Directly from the definition, T(p,q,r) holds iff one of the following holds:
- two of p, q, r are ∞ and the third is ∞;
- exactly one of them is ∞ and the other two are equal;
- none is ∞, and either p = q = r, or p, q, r are three distinct collinear points.

Check of the case "none is ∞": if p = q then p⊞q = {∞, p}, so r = p; if p ≠ q, then r ∈ ℓ(p,q) \ {p,q}. Each condition in the list is symmetric in p, q, r, so T is totally symmetric. This gives:
- 0_H-uniqueness: ∞ ∈ a⊞b ⇔ T(a,b,∞) ⇔ a = b. So the negative of a is unique and equals a.
- Reversibility: c ∈ a⊞b ⇔ T(a,b,c) ⇔ T(c,b,a) ⇔ a ∈ c⊞b = c⊞(-b).

*Associativity.* Put R(a,b,c,e) :⇔ (a⊞b) ∩ (c⊞e) ≠ ∅, i.e. ∃t: T(a,b,t) ∧ T(c,e,t).

We have e ∈ (a⊞b)⊞c ⇔ ∃t ∈ a⊞b with e ∈ t⊞c ⇔ ∃t ∈ a⊞b with t ∈ e⊞c (symmetry of T) ⇔ R(a,b,c,e). Likewise e ∈ a⊞(b⊞c) = (b⊞c)⊞a ⇔ R(b,c,a,e). By definition R is invariant under a↔b, under c↔e, and under swapping the two pairs. So associativity follows once R depends only on the multiset {a,b,c,e}. This means checking that the three pairings {ab|ce}, {ac|be}, {ae|bc} agree.

- *Some entry is ∞*, say e = ∞. Then R(a,b,c,∞) ⇔ ∃t: T(a,b,t) ∧ t = c ⇔ T(a,b,c). The pairing {a∞|bc} gives ∃t: t = a ∧ T(b,c,t) ⇔ T(a,b,c) as well. Since T is symmetric, every pairing is equivalent to T of the other three entries. This also covers the cases with several ∞'s.

- *All entries in A, pairwise distinct.* Then t = ∞ is impossible, and so is t ∈ {a,b}. So R(a,b,c,e) ⇔ (ℓ(a,b) \ {a,b}) ∩ (ℓ(c,e) \ {c,e}) ≠ ∅.
  - If all four points are collinear on m, every pairing gives m \ {a,b,c,e} ≠ ∅. This is true for every pairing, since |m| ≥ 5 in our application; in general the condition "|m| ≥ 5" is the same for all pairings.
  - If exactly three are collinear, say a, b, c on m and e ∉ m, then in every pairing one pair spans m and the other pair is {p, e} with p ∈ m. The line ℓ(p,e) meets m only in p, and p is excluded. So every pairing is false.
  - If no three are collinear, ℓ(a,b) ≠ ℓ(c,e) meet in a point q (P2), and q ∉ {a,b,c,e}: for example q = a would make a, c, e collinear. So every pairing is true.

- *Multiset {a,a,c,e}* with a, c, e ∈ A pairwise distinct.
  - {aa|ce}: {∞,a} ∩ (c⊞e) ≠ ∅ ⇔ a ∈ c⊞e ⇔ a, c, e collinear.
  - {ac|ae}: if a, c, e lie on a line m, the intersection is m \ {a,c,e}, which is nonempty by (P3). Otherwise ℓ(a,c) ∩ ℓ(a,e) = {a}, and a is excluded.
  - So both pairings say "a, c, e collinear".

- *Multiset {a,a,c,c}*, a ≠ c. Both pairings are true: {∞,a} ∩ {∞,c} ∋ ∞, and a⊞c ≠ ∅.

- *Multiset {a,a,a,e}* (only one pairing) and *{a,a,a,a}* (only one pairing): nothing to check.

So R is symmetric, ⊞ is associative, and H is a hyperfield. ∎

(For the record: from memory, this is the classical construction of a hypergroup from a projective geometry with at least 4 points per line, due to Prenowitz and Lyndon and used by Connes–Consani for extensions of the Krasner hyperfield. The proof above is self-contained and does not rely on that citation.)

## 2. Failure of the claim in such a plane

**Lemma 2.** In the setting of Lemma 1, suppose x, y ∈ A satisfy the following (additive notation, so 1 = 0, x^3 = 3x, xy = x+y, y^3 = 3y):
- (i) 0, x, y are distinct and collinear;
- (ii) 0, 3x, x+y are distinct and lie on a line L;
- (iii) 3y ∉ L.

Then, with z = 1 (the element 0 of A), we have 0_H ∈ x⊞y⊞z, but 0_H ∉ x^3⊞y^3⊞z^3⊞(-xyz)⊞(-xyz)⊞(-xyz).

*Proof.* The hypothesis: x⊞y = ℓ(x,y) \ {x,y} contains the point 0 by (i). Hence ∞ ∈ x⊞y⊞0.

The target: since -1 = 1 and z = 1, the target sum is S = T ⊞ 1, where T = x^3⊞y^3⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy. For a set U, ∞ ∈ U ⊞ 1 ⇔ 1 ∈ U, so it suffices to show 1 ∉ T.

We have xy⊞xy = {∞, xy}, and then xy⊞xy⊞xy = (∞⊞xy) ∪ (xy⊞xy) = {∞, xy}. Hence T = (x^3⊞y^3) ∪ ((x^3⊞y^3)⊞xy).

Let M = ℓ(3x, 3y); note 3x ≠ 3y because 3y ∉ L ∋ 3x. Since 3y ∉ L, M ≠ L, and the two lines meet exactly in 3x.
- 1 ∈ x^3⊞y^3 = M \ {3x,3y} would put the point 0 on M. But 0 ∈ L and 0 ≠ 3x, so 0 ∉ M.
- 1 ∈ (x^3⊞y^3)⊞xy ⇔ ∃t ∈ x^3⊞y^3 with 1 ∈ t⊞xy ⇔ ∃t ∈ (x^3⊞y^3) ∩ (1⊞xy), by reversibility. Here x^3⊞y^3 = M \ {3x,3y}. Also 1⊞xy = L \ {0, x+y}, since L is the line through 0 and x+y. Now M ∩ L = {3x}, and 3x is excluded from M \ {3x,3y}. So the intersection is empty.

Hence 1 ∉ T, and the target fails. ∎

Remark (consistency check): in Desarguesian planes coming from quotients F_{q^3}/F_q^*, write x' + y' = 1. Then y'^3 = 1 - x'^3 - 3x'y' lies in the span of 1, x'^3, x'y'. So (ii) forces y^3 ∈ L, and (iii) cannot hold. This agrees with (A3).

## 3. A free planar difference set realizing (i)–(iii)

Translation-invariant planes on A with a single line orbit are given by a set D ⊂ A with:
- **(Sidon)** d1 - d2 = d3 - d4 with d1 ≠ d2 and d3 ≠ d4 forces (d1,d2) = (d3,d4);
- **(Cover)** D - D = A.

**Lemma 3.** If D is infinite and satisfies (Sidon) and (Cover), then 𝓛 = {D + h : h ∈ A} satisfies (P1)–(P4).

*Proof.*
- (P4) is clear.
- Distinct h give distinct lines: if D + h = D + h' with h ≠ h', then w = h' - h ≠ 0 and D + w = D. Then (d + w) - d = w for every d ∈ D, giving two different pairs with the same difference, contrary to (Sidon).
- (P1): for points p ≠ q, the line D + h contains both iff (q - h, p - h) is a pair in D with difference q - p. By (Cover) and (Sidon) there is exactly one such pair, and it determines h.
- (P2): lines D + h ≠ D + h' meet in p iff p - h, p - h' ∈ D. These two elements differ by h' - h ≠ 0, and there is exactly one pair (d, d') in D with d - d' = h' - h. So there is exactly one common point p = d + h.
- (P3): D is infinite. ∎

**Construction.**
- Let A_0 = Z^3 with free generators X, Y, u.
- Let D_0 = {0, X, Y, u, u+3X, u+X+Y}.

D_0 is Sidon. The differences inside {0,X,Y} are ±X, ±Y, ±(X-Y). The differences inside {u, u+3X, u+X+Y} are ±3X, ±(X+Y), ±(2X-Y). The cross differences are ±(u + s - f) with s ∈ {0, 3X, X+Y} and f ∈ {0, X, Y}. The nine values of s - f are 0, -X, -Y, 3X, 2X, 3X-Y, X+Y, Y, X, which are pairwise distinct. The cross differences have u-coefficient ±1, the others have u-coefficient 0. So all 30 ordered differences are distinct.

*Extension step.* Suppose D_n ⊂ A_n is a finite Sidon set, and a ∈ A_n \ ({0} ∪ (D_n - D_n)). Put A_{n+1} = A_n ⊕ Z t_n (t_n a new free generator) and D_{n+1} = D_n ∪ {t_n, t_n + a}. Then D_{n+1} is Sidon and a ∈ D_{n+1} - D_{n+1}. The new differences are ±a, ±(t_n - d) and ±(t_n + a - d) for d ∈ D_n.
- ±a are not old differences, because D_n - D_n is symmetric and a is not in it. Also a ≠ -a, since the group is torsion-free.
- The differences containing t_n differ from all others by their t_n-coefficient.
- Among themselves, a coincidence t_n - d = t_n + a - d' gives a = d' - d. This is either 0 or an element of D_n - D_n, which is excluded.
- Coincidences t_n - d = t_n - d' and t_n + a - d = t_n + a - d' force d = d'.

*Dovetailing.* When A_i is created, fix an enumeration (a_{i,k})_k of it; A_i is countable. Fix a bijection N → N×N, n ↦ (i(n), k(n)), with i(n) ≤ n (e.g. the inverse of the Cantor pairing).
- At stage n, look at a = a_{i(n),k(n)} ∈ A_{i(n)} ⊆ A_n.
- If a ≠ 0 and a ∉ D_n - D_n, apply the extension step.
- Otherwise put A_{n+1} = A_n and D_{n+1} = D_n.

Let A = ∪ A_n, which is free abelian of countable rank, hence abelian and torsion-free, and let D = ∪ D_n.
- D is Sidon, because any two pairs lie in a common D_n.
- D satisfies (Cover): every nonzero a ∈ A equals some a_{i,k}, and this element is treated at the stage n with (i(n),k(n)) = (i,k).
- D is infinite, since D - D = A is infinite.

By Lemmas 3 and 1, the lines D + h make H = A ∪ {∞} a hyperfield.

**Verification of (i)–(iii).** Take x = X and y = Y.
- (i) 0, X, Y ∈ D are distinct and lie on the line D.
- (ii) The line L = D - u contains u - u = 0, (u+3X) - u = 3X and (u+X+Y) - u = X+Y. These three points are distinct.
- (iii) 3Y ∈ L ⇔ 3Y + u ∈ D. The element 3Y + u lies in A_0. It is not in D_0, and every element of D \ D_0 has a nonzero coefficient on some t_n, so it is not in A_0. Hence 3Y ∉ L.

Key point: free extension steps only add *new* points to D. Incidences among the old points of A_0 are never changed.

By Lemma 2, in this hyperfield we have 0 ∈ x⊞y⊞z for x = X, y = Y, z = 1, but 0 ∉ x^3⊞y^3⊞z^3⊞-xyz⊞-xyz⊞-xyz.

## 4. Summary

**Proved.** The answer to the Question is **No**. The counterexample is a hyperfield H = A ∪ {0}, where:

# Answer to round4_q6: the answer is NO (a complete counterexample)

**Plan / status.** I did not follow the free-hyperfield chase. A much more explicit counterexample exists, so I went straight to it. It is a "Krasner-type" hyperfield (-1 = 1, a⊞a = {0,a}) built from an **infinite cyclic projective plane**, which in turn comes from a perfect difference set in Z (M. Hall's greedy construction; that construction is reproved below). The coordinator's remark (C3) looked only at finite geometries, which are all Desarguesian. Infinite cyclic planes are not Desarguesian in general, and that is where the counterexample lives. Every step below is proved in full.

**Theorem.** There is a hyperfield H with elements x, y, z such that 0 ∈ x⊞y⊞z but 0 ∉ x³⊞y³⊞z³⊞(-xyz)⊞(-xyz)⊞(-xyz). Equivalently, (N) fails.

## 1. A perfect difference set

**Lemma 1.** Let D_0 = {0,1,3,20,24,29}. There is a set D ⊆ Z with D ⊇ D_0 such that every nonzero integer n can be written in exactly one way as n = d - d' with d, d' ∈ D.

*Proof.* Call a finite set S ⊂ Z *Sidon* if the differences d - d' (d ≠ d' in S) are pairwise distinct.

D_0 is Sidon. Its 15 positive differences are 1,3,2,20,19,17,24,23,21,4,29,28,26,9,5, and these are pairwise distinct.

Construct D_k inductively. Given a finite Sidon set D_k, let m_k be the least positive integer that is not a difference of D_k. Let M = max_{d∈D_k}|d|, choose an integer a > 2M + m_k, and set D_{k+1} = D_k ∪ {a, a+m_k}.

The positive differences of D_{k+1} that are not differences of D_k are:
- m_k;
- a - d for d ∈ D_k;
- a + m_k - d for d ∈ D_k.

They are pairwise distinct and distinct from the old differences:
- Every old difference is ≤ 2M.
- Each a - d and each a + m_k - d is ≥ a - M > M + m_k, so it exceeds both 2M... more precisely it exceeds M + m_k ≥ m_k and exceeds every old difference (≤ 2M < a - M).
- m_k is not an old difference, by its choice.
- The values a - d are pairwise distinct, and so are the values a + m_k - d.
- If a - d = a + m_k - d', then d' - d = m_k. This is impossible: m_k > 0 is not a difference of D_k.

So D_{k+1} is Sidon, and m_k is now a difference. Every integer below m_k was already a difference of D_k, so m_{k+1} > m_k. Hence every positive integer is a difference of some D_k.

Let D = ∪_k D_k. Every positive integer n is a difference d - d' in D. Then -n = d' - d, so every nonzero integer is a difference.

Uniqueness: two representations of the same n would already lie in some finite D_k, which is Sidon. ∎

D is infinite. Note in particular **23 ∉ D**. Otherwise 3 = 23 - 20 and 3 = 3 - 0 would be two different representations of 3.

## 2. The cyclic plane

Points are the integers. Lines are the translates t + D (t ∈ Z).

**Lemma 2.**
- (L1) Two distinct points lie on exactly one line.
- (L2) Two distinct lines meet in exactly one point.
- (L3) Every line is infinite.
- (L4) Translation maps lines to lines.

*Proof.*

(L4) is clear, and (L3) holds because D is infinite.

Distinct t give distinct lines. Suppose t + D = t' + D with t ≠ t'. Then d + (t - t') ∈ D for every d ∈ D, so t - t' has more than one representation as a difference. That contradicts Lemma 1.

(L1) Let a ≠ b. A line t + D contains both a and b iff a - t, b - t ∈ D. Their difference is b - a, which equals d - d' for a unique pair (d, d'). So b - t = d and a - t = d', which forces t = a - d'. This t works, so the line exists and is unique.

(L2) Take two lines t + D and t' + D with t ≠ t'. A common point p satisfies p - t, p - t' ∈ D, and (p - t') - (p - t) = t - t'. Write t - t' uniquely as d - d'. Then p - t' = d, so p is unique, and p = t' + d does lie on both lines. ∎

## 3. The hyperfield

Let G = ⟨θ⟩ be infinite cyclic, with θ^n identified with the point n. Put H = G ∪ {0}, with 0 absorbing for multiplication. Write L(a,b) for the line through distinct a, b ∈ G. Define addition by:
- 0⊞a = a⊞0 = {a};
- a⊞a = {0, a} for a ∈ G;
- a⊞b = L(a,b) \ {a,b} for distinct a, b ∈ G.

So -a = a.

**Lemma 3.** H is a hyperfield.

*Proof.* We check the axioms in turn.

1. **Commutativity** is clear.

2. **Nonempty sums.** a⊞b is nonempty because lines are infinite (L3).

3. **Neutral element and negatives.** 0 is neutral. For a, b ∈ G we have 0 ∈ a⊞b iff a = b, because a⊞b ⊆ G when a ≠ b. So negatives are unique, and -a = a.

4. **Reversibility.** Since -b = b, we must show: c ∈ a⊞b ⇒ a ∈ c⊞b.
   - If a = 0, then c = b, and 0 ∈ b⊞b.
   - If b = 0, then c = a, and a ∈ a⊞0.
   - If c = 0, then a = b, and a ∈ 0⊞a.
   - If a, b, c ∈ G and a = b, then c = a, and a ∈ a⊞a.
   - If a, b, c ∈ G and a ≠ b, then c ∈ L(a,b) with c ≠ a, b. So L(c,b) = L(a,b), and a lies on this line with a ≠ c, b. Hence a ∈ c⊞b.

   With commutativity this gives: the relation Z3(a,b,c) :⇔ c ∈ a⊞b is invariant under all permutations of a, b, c. For a, b, c ∈ G, Z3(a,b,c) holds iff either a = b = c, or a, b, c are distinct and collinear.

5. **Distributivity.** Multiplication by θ^k is a translation, and translations map lines to lines (L4), so g·L(a,b) = L(ga,gb). Hence g(a⊞b) = ga⊞gb for g ∈ G. For w = 0, both sides equal {0}, since a⊞b ≠ ∅.

6. **Associativity.** We use the four-point criterion.

   *Reduction.* Since -1 = 1 and reversibility holds, e ∈ t⊞c ⇔ t ∈ e⊞c. Therefore
   - e ∈ (a⊞b)⊞c ⇔ R(a,b|c,e), where R(a,b|c,e) means (a⊞b)∩(c⊞e) ≠ ∅;
   - e ∈ a⊞(b⊞c) = (b⊞c)⊞a ⇔ R(b,c|a,e).

   So it suffices to show that R(a,b|c,e) depends only on the multiset {a,b,c,e}, and not on how it is split into two pairs.

   *If the multiset contains 0.* Suppose the pairing puts 0 with u, and the other pair is v, w. Then 0⊞u = {u}, so R ⇔ u ∈ v⊞w ⇔ Z3(u,v,w). Here {u,v,w} is the multiset with one 0 removed, so the result is independent of the pairing.

   *If a, b, c, e ∈ G.* There are five cases.
   - {a,a,a,a}: every pairing gives {0,a}∩{0,a}, which is nonempty, so all pairings are true.
   - {a,a,a,b} with b ≠ a: every pairing is {aa|ab}, giving {0,a}∩(L(a,b)\{a,b}) = ∅. So all pairings are false.
   - {a,a,b,b}: the pairing {aa|bb} gives a set containing 0. The pairing {ab|ab} gives a⊞b ≠ ∅. So all pairings are true.
   - {a,a,b,c} with a, b, c distinct:
     - The pairing {aa|bc} holds iff a ∈ L(b,c).
     - The pairing {ab|ac} is (L(a,b)\{a,b})∩(L(a,c)\{a,c}). If a, b, c are collinear, this is the line minus three points, which is nonempty. Otherwise two distinct lines meet only at a, which is excluded, so it is empty.
     - Both pairings therefore hold iff a, b, c are collinear.
   - a, b, c, e distinct:
     - If all four are collinear on a line L, every pairing gives L \ {a,b,c,e} ≠ ∅, so all are true.
     - Otherwise L(a,b) ≠ L(c,e). By (L2) they meet in a single point p, and R(a,b|c,e) ⇔ p ∉ {a,b,c,e}. Now p = a ⇔ a, c, e are collinear. Likewise p = b ⇔ b, c, e collinear; p = c ⇔ a, b, c collinear; p = e ⇔ a, b, e collinear.
     - So in this case R holds iff no three of the four points are collinear, which is symmetric in a, b, c, e.

   In all cases R depends only on the multiset, so ⊞ is associative. ∎

## 4. The counterexample

Take x = θ, y = θ³, z = 1. Then x³ = θ³, y³ = θ⁹, z³ = 1, and -xyz = xyz = θ⁴.

**Hypothesis.** 0 ∈ (x⊞y)⊞1 ⇔ 1 ∈ θ⊞θ³ ⇔ the points 0, 1, 3 are distinct and collinear. This holds because they all lie in D.

**Target.** The target sum is the six-term sum θ³⊞θ⁹⊞1⊞θ⁴⊞θ⁴⊞θ⁴. First, θ⁴⊞θ⁴⊞θ⁴ = {0,θ⁴}⊞θ⁴ = {θ⁴}∪{0,θ⁴} = {0,θ⁴}. Put A = θ³⊞θ⁹⊞1. Then the target sum is A⊞{0,θ⁴} = A ∪ (A⊞θ⁴). So 0 lies in it iff one of the following holds:

- **(i) 0 ∈ A.** This holds iff 1 ∈ θ³⊞θ⁹, i.e. iff the points 0, 3, 9 are collinear.
  - The line through 0 and 9: we have 9 = 29 - 20, so this line is -20 + D, and it contains 0, 4, 9.
  - 3 lies on -20 + D iff 23 ∈ D, which is false (end of §1).
  - So (i) fails.
- **(ii) θ⁴ ∈ A.** This holds iff (θ³⊞θ⁹)∩(1⊞θ⁴) ≠ ∅, by the reduction in §3, step 6.
  - Here 1⊞θ⁴ = (-20+D) \ {0,4} and θ³⊞θ⁹ = L(3,9) \ {3,9}.
  - These two lines are distinct, because 3 ∉ -20 + D. They share the point 9, so by (L2) they meet only at 9.
  - But 9 ∉ θ³⊞θ⁹. So the intersection is empty and (ii) fails.

Hence 0 ∉ x³⊞y³⊞z³⊞(-xyz)⊞(-xyz)⊞(-xyz), although 0 ∈ x⊞y⊞z. The answer to the question is **NO**.

In the normalized form (N): with x = θ, y = θ³ we have 1 ∈ x⊞y. But 1 ∉ T = x³⊞y³⊞xy⊞xy⊞xy, because 1 ∈ T ⇔ 0 ∈ T⊞1, which is exactly the set just shown not to contain 0.

## 5. Remarks (consistency checks; not needed for the proof)

- **The configuration.** Write 1, x³, y³, xy for the points 0, 3, 9, 4. Exactly one triple among them is collinear, namely {1, y³, xy}. For a hyperfield of this type, that is precisely the failure condition.
- **Consistency with (A3).** By (A3), quotient hyperfields satisfy the claim. So this H is not a quotient of a field, and correspondingly the plane is not Desarguesian.
- **Consistency with (C1).** Finite cyclic planes with lines of at least 4 points have |G| ≥ 13. This fits the search result (C1), which found no counterexample with |G| ≤ 9.
- **Consistency with B-3(i).** H also violates the core claim (C): 1 ∉ x³⊞y³⊞xy.
- **Literature.** Infinite cyclic projective planes are due to M. Hall Jr., "Cyclic projective planes" (Duke Math. J., 1947). The link between such planes and hyperfields with a⊞a = {0,a} is due to Connes–Consani. Both are cited from memory only. Every fact used here is proved above.
- **Open questions.** None for the posed question. The free-hyperfield construction suggested in the query was not needed and was not carried out.

triangles {g, gx, gx^2w} (g ∈ G) are relations.

**Lemma 1.1.** 1⊞1⊞1⊞w⊞w⊞w = A⊞A⊞A, and the claim (1 ∈ T) holds iff 0 ∈ A⊞A⊞A iff (A⊞A) ∩ A ≠ ∅.
Moreover A⊞A = {0} ∪ D ∪ wD ∪ (D⊞wD), so the claim holds iff A∩D ≠ ∅ or A∩wD ≠ ∅ or A∩(D⊞wD) ≠ ∅.
*Proof.* Regroup the six summands as (1⊞w)⊞(1⊞w)⊞(1⊞w) (associativity/commutativity); by (A4) the claim is
0 ∈ 1⊞1⊞1⊞w⊞w⊞w. 0 ∈ A⊞(A⊞A) iff A ∩ (A⊞A) ≠ ∅ (since -1 = 1). Finally A⊞A = (1⊞1)⊞(w⊞w) with
1⊞1 = {0}∪D, w⊞w = {0}∪wD. ∎

**Lemma 1.2 (sufficient criterion).** If A ∩ dA ≠ ∅ for some d ∈ D, the claim holds.
*Proof.* Take a, da ∈ A. Since d ∈ 1⊞1, da ∈ a⊞a, so 0 ∈ a⊞a⊞da ⊆ A⊞A⊞A. ∎

**Lemma 1.3.** Let K := {c ∈ G : A ∩ cA ≠ ∅} = A·A^{-1}. Then K ⊇ {x^i w^j : i ∈ {1,2}, j ∈ {0,1,2}}.
*Proof.* The triangles {1, x, x^2w} and {x, x^2, w} share x, so x ∈ (1⊞x^2w) ∩ (x^2⊞w), i.e.
0 ∈ 1⊞x^2w⊞x^2⊞w. Re-pairing (four-point form of associativity, A5(c)): (1⊞w) ∩ (x^2⊞x^2w) ≠ ∅, i.e.
A ∩ x^2A ≠ ∅; so x^2 ∈ K, and K = K^{-1} gives x ∈ K. The triangles {1,x,x^2w} and
x^2w·{1,x,x^2w} = {x^2w, w, xw^2} share x^2w; so 0 ∈ 1⊞x⊞w⊞xw^2, and re-pairing (1,w)|(x,xw^2) gives
A ∩ x(1⊞w^2) ≠ ∅; as 1⊞w^2 = w^2(w⊞1) = w^2A, xw^2 ∈ K. The triangles {1,x,x^2w} and xw·{1,x,x^2w} =
{xw, x^2w, w^2} share x^2w; so 0 ∈ 1⊞x⊞xw⊞w^2, and re-pairing (1,w^2)|(x,xw) gives w^2A ∩ xA ≠ ∅, so

in every hyperfield. (Pairs with a=0 or b=0 are trivial: then the other is 1 and the target is 1 ∈ 1.)

## Change of first move (recorded honestly)
The thin-class classification (1⊞1={0,p}) quickly led only to quotients (F_5/{±1}, F_7/{±1}); abandoned.
New first move: **twisting the multiplication of a field-quotient hyperfield by a Dickson-type cocycle**
(equivalently: quotients of Dickson near-fields by a normal subgroup containing the commutator subgroup).
Why this escapes (F1)/(F8): the resulting hyperfields have the *same addition* as a quotient F/C of a field but a
*different multiplication*; (N) mixes multiplication and addition non-linearly, and these hyperfields are not
quotients of fields, so (F8) gives no protection. Whether (N) holds there is a concrete finite computation.

### Construction T(q, C) (twisted quotient)
Let q be an odd prime power, F = F_{q^2}, σ(a) = a^q, S = F^{*2} the squares, ν(a) = 0 if a ∈ S and 1 otherwise,
μ = μ_{q+1} = ker(norm), C0 = μ^2 = μ_{(q+1)/2}. Let C be a subgroup of S with C ∩ μ = C0, G0 = F^*/C, and
η := the class of g^{q-1} (g a generator of F^*); η ∉ C-class, η^2 = 1, ν(η) = 0.
Fact: for a ∈ F^*, a^{q-1} ∈ C iff a ∈ S, and a^{q-1} ∈ ηC iff a ∉ S. (a = g^k: a^{q-1} = (g^{q-1})^k ∈ μ, and lies
in C0 = μ^2 iff k is even.)  Hence σ acts on G0 by σ(X) = X η^{ν(X)}.
Define on H = G0 ∪ {0}: X ⊞ Y := the addition of the quotient hyperfield F/C, and
  X * Y := X Y η^{ν(X)ν(Y)}.
Claim: (H, ⊞, *) is a hyperfield.
 * (G0, *) is an abelian group: commutative (symmetric exponent), associative since both bracketings give exponent
   ν(X)ν(Y)+ν(X)ν(Z)+ν(Y)ν(Z) (using ν(XY η^…) = ν(X)+ν(Y), as ν(η)=0); identity 1; inverses exist.
 * Additive axioms are those of F/C.
 * Distributivity: if ν(Z)=0, Z*W = ZW and multiplication by a class is an automorphism of F/C. If ν(Z)=1,
   Z*W = Z W η^{ν(W)} = Z σ(W), and W ↦ σ(W) is the automorphism of F/C induced by the field automorphism σ
   (σ(C)=C). So Z*(X⊞Y) = Zσ(X⊞Y) = Zσ(X) ⊞ Zσ(Y) = Z*X ⊞ Z*Y.
(Equivalently H = N/C for the Dickson near-field N of order q^2.)
In H: X^{*3} = X^3 η^{ν(X)}, X*Y = XY η^{ν(X)ν(Y)}.
So (N) fails in H iff there are a, b ∈ F with a + b = 1 such that
 (i) ν(a)=ν(b)=1 and the class η is NOT in [a^3] ⊞ [b^3] ⊞ [ab] ⊞ [ab] ⊞ [ab] (computed in F/C), or
 (ii) ν(a)=1, ν(b)=0 and 1 ∉ η[a^3] ⊞ [b^3] ⊞ [ab] ⊞ [ab] ⊞ [ab].
(The hypothesis 1 ∈ X ⊞ Y can be normalised to a + b = 1 with a ∈ X, b ∈ Y by multiplying by an element of C.)
Check q = 3 (|H| = 5): C = {±1}, η = {±i}; the only case (i) pair is a = -1+i, b = -1-i, and
a^3 - b^3 = -2i = i ∈ η, so (N) holds there (consistent with (F8)'s search).
